builderWarmUp.appliesOnWhy: PERMANENT: Windows builds natively. PlantoirSetup.exe carries its whole runtime and nothing is downloaded or built for building (documentation/12-windows-app.md, the like-for-like table), so there is no builder to get ready in the background.
builderWarmUp.launcher: setup.sh --prepare-builder, run from ~/Library/Application Support/Plantoir/getting-ready, which holds that launcher and a mirror of the recipe made by the same function that mirrors a working folder's .toolchain, so the image built is the one every working folder's launchers look for (its tag is a hash of the recipe). It installs what the builder needs, starts it and builds it, then stops: no courses folder, no workspace, no builds folder. `setup.sh --builder-tag` prints BUILDER_TAG=<name> for the same recipe and starts nothing.
builderWarmUp.note: Getting the website builder ready in the background at first launch, and at the first launch of each new version, so the first preview is fast (bundle B; Russell's change of 2026-09-26, which replaced a 'decision' issue). The mac only, permanently: Windows carries its runtime and builds natively, with nothing to download or build first (appliesOn).
builderWarmUp.record: getting-ready/ready-for.txt holds the builder's name ('teaching-quartz:src-55e586fe') from the BUILDER_READY= line of the last run that printed it. A run that did not is not recorded, so the next launch tries again. At launch the app asks `setup.sh --builder-tag` (which starts nothing) for the name the recipe it carries would have, and warms up only when the two differ.
rejected: Waiting in the app: a preview started from the command line, the assistant's server or a scheduled publish would not wait, and 'the app remembers to' is the kind of rule that is forgotten at the next new entry point. The launchers are where every path meets.
A status window or a progress bar: background work the teacher did not ask for gets one plain line.
Waiting for a working folder to be chosen: the folder's .toolchain exists only once it holds a course, and the wizard is the time this spends.
Stopping it at quit: what it downloaded would be wasted, and #220's quit path already leaves the builder running while any launcher is.
Asking first: Russell's decision, 2026-09-26, that the download may happen before the teacher asks (the plan had proposed it as a decision).

turn.rule: One launcher at a time starts the builder and builds it. The turn is taken (mkdir) before the builder is started and handed back as soon as the image is ready - never held through a build of a site or a publish; deploy.sh hands it back after starting the builder and takes it again only if it has to build the image to make a workspace. It holds the holder's process id. A turn is taken over when its holder is not running, when the process now holding its id started AFTER the turn was taken (the id was reused), or when it is older than a ceiling (two hours); one with no id yet is waited on for a minute. Handed back on any exit.

A deploy builds first when the file is missing, empty, or names another toolchain: deploy.sh compares it with its own $IMAGE and runs preview.sh --build-only (which remakes an out-of-date workspace); deploy.ps1's folder publish asks toolchain_paths.site_was_built_by_this_toolchain and builds first on anything but a plain yes (#749); deploy.py compares it with its own toolchain in ensure_base_url_and_rebuild, the one place both destinations decide to rebuild, so a deploy builds at most once. BuildFreshness in the apps does NOT read it: the deploy itself decides, so every caller - the window, the assistant, a scheduled deploy, the command line - is covered by one check. Measured 2026-11-01: a site redeployed under 1.9.1 served 1.9.0's stylesheet without it. Every site built before 1.9.2 has no file, and is built once on its next deploy. Since #768 the launchers ask the PAGES too, in the same decision and after this question (toolchain_paths.why_build_before_deploying, deploy.sh's pages_or_clock_ask_for_a_build): `reuseTheLastBuild` is the whole rule. A workspace that does not carry PLANTOIR_TOOLCHAIN_ID=<its image's tag> (made by hand, or by an older verify.sh) is made again once by preview.sh and setup.sh (#748 part 3, the reason toolchainId), since every site built in it would otherwise be stamped with something else and built again on every deploy.

previewBuild.note: One rule for 'this built site is a preview's', read by every checker: BuildFreshness in each app, the mac's scheduled publish (its own shell check, because the app is closed when it runs), deploy.sh (three times), deploy.py and deploy.ps1. Serve mode bakes the live-reload client into EVERY page and the built tree is replaced file by file, so a clean front page in front of a preview's pages is a real state — deploy.sh found it on 2026-09-05 and has read the whole tree since, as has deploy.py. The apps read the front page alone until issue #136: they called that state deploy-fresh, skipped their build, and the LAUNCHER then rebuilt under the destination's leg — the build's milestones missing from the panel, and on the mac a question the build asked overnight reported as the destination's. A reader narrower than the launchers is the fault, whichever side it is on. Issue #291 then narrowed WHAT is looked for: the bare address matched any page that mentions it, and the rule is now the client's tag and first statement (`signature`). Each case is a tree under the section's public/ folder; `unreadable` names pages that exist but cannot be opened; `invalidUTF8Before` names pages that begin with the bytes FF 0A, which are not UTF-8.
previewBuild.notShared: Three things are deliberately NOT cases. (2) Upper-case .HTML, and a public/ that is ITSELF a symbolic link (neither FileManager's enumerator nor grep -r descends into one; a link further up, such as the mac's .merged_output, is followed by both — measured): Quartz produces neither. deploy.ps1 still matches its old signature without regard to case (Select-String's default); once it adopts this rule it must match case-SENSITIVELY, which is owed on #272. (3) A page whose teacher typed the client verbatim as raw HTML (the tag and the client, unescaped): that page really does open a socket to the reader's machine, so calling it a preview's is not wrong, and no fixture would say anything cases 13 and 14 do not. (A page that is not valid UTF-8 used to be listed here, erring safe; with a whole-page read the miss erred UNSAFE, so it is case 15 since #291.)

signature.betweenNote: Any run of these bytes, including none, and nothing else: POSIX [[:space:]] in the C locale. Not a Unicode \s, which in .NET and in Python's str patterns also takes non-breaking and other spaces.
signature.why: (#291) The bare address ws://localhost: was the rule until 2026-09-26, and it is in ANY page whose note mentions it: measured in a production build of stock Quartz v4.5.0, one networking lesson carried it 20 times on 7 lines (title, meta tags, breadcrumb, heading, prose, code), so a folder publish refused after 30 s every time and every other publish rebuilt. The rule is now the client's script TAG followed by its first statement with only `between` bytes in between. A page's words cannot produce that: Quartz writes < as < in text AND in attribute values (measured: content="<script type="…"), so a raw <script can only come from raw HTML a teacher typed. Narrower strings were measured and rejected: new WebSocket('ws://localhost: matches a meta description (' is not escaped in attributes), inline code and an un-languaged fence; const socket = new WebSocket('ws://localhost: matches inline code and the fence; 'the tag and the client both appear somewhere' is wrong because a production page already holds the same tag for Quartz's own inline script (case 10). Quartz writes the tag and the client on DIFFERENT lines, so a line reader must read each page as ONE record (grep -z, PowerShell -Raw), and grep -z needs LC_ALL=C: under a UTF-8 locale BSD grep -z misses the client in a file holding an invalid byte anywhere BEFORE the client — in practice nearly the whole page, since Quartz writes the client at the end of <body> (case 15), which is the unsafe direction. Source: Quartz v4.5.0 quartz/plugins/index.ts:26-38 and quartz/util/resources.tsx:26; raising Quartz means re-measuring this, and verify.sh and verify-deploy.sh fail when those bytes move.

previewBuild.where: Every file whose name ends .html anywhere under the section's built public/ folder, hidden folders included, compared as bytes and read as ONE record, not line by line: the tag and the client are on different lines. The front page first, so a real preview's build answers from one file. A page that cannot be opened is passed over, as every launcher does.

reuseTheLastBuild.casesShape: Every case starts from the same course unless it gives `course`: the files in `theCourse` (folders made as their paths need), and the hidden link .merged_output to the folder outside the course that holds section1, as the launchers keep built sites. The course and the built section are made in this order on the real clock, with a pause between each step so each has its own time: the course; the changes `beforeTheBuildStarted`; then for `startedMarker` beforeTheSite (the default) the start marker, the changes `whileItBuilt`, the front page; for afterTheSite the front page, the changes `whileItBuilt`, the start marker; for absent the changes `whileItBuilt`, then the front page; then the changes `afterTheBuild`. `atTheBuildStart` edits the file just before the marker is written and then gives the marker exactly the file's modification time. `datedLaterThanNow` moves the marker and the front page one hour ahead, keeping their order, before the `afterTheBuild` changes. `site` notBuilt makes no front page and no marker. `previewClient` writes a preview's front page (`previewBuild.signature.asQuartzWritesIt` in a body). `courseFolderIsALink` makes the course in a folder elsewhere and links courses/C to it, and makes the older copy beside it before the build; a reader that cannot make links (Windows without Developer Mode) skips these cases and says so. `stamp` is this (the default: the reader's own toolchain), another, or missing. A change `do`es one of: edit (add a line to the file where it is), delete, rename (to `to`), replaceKeepingItsOldTime (a new copy written beside it, given the old file's modification time, and moved over it), overwriteKeepingItsOldTime (rewritten in place, then given back its old modification time), createKeepingAnOldTime (a new file dated a year ago), pointTheLinkAtAnOlderCopy (for `courseFolderIsALink`: the link made again, under a temporary name renamed over it as `ln -sfn` does, pointing at a copy of the course made before the build, with other words and the same built sites). `expect` is reuse or build, and `because` the reason when it builds. `inTheApps` replaces both for the readers that do not read the stamp. `typedByHand` refused: deploy.sh refuses before it asks. `knownLimitOn` names a platform whose readers skip the case, with `knownLimits` saying why.
knownLimits: A file system that keeps times to the second (HFS+) or two seconds (exFAT) can date a save made in the same second as the build's start no later than the start, and it then reads as built. The working folder has to be in the home folder on a Mac (#221), which is APFS there; on Windows an exFAT drive is possible.

Anything that changes a file's metadata without changing what students see costs one build that was not needed: a Finder tag, a quarantine flag, a sync service's own marks, macOS noting when a file was last opened. So does a hidden file or folder being created, removed or replaced in ANY folder of the course (.publish_state, .netlify_sites or .cloudflare_sites at the top the first time, a .DS_Store Finder writes, an editor's swap file), because that folder's own time changes. Each errs toward building, once.

A symbolic link INSIDE the course is not followed, by any reader: a folder linked in from elsewhere (a section folder kept outside the course, say) changes behind its link and reads as built, while the build follows it. Such a link POINTED at another folder is seen (its own times change, and they are read). The course folder ITSELF being a link is followed (`courseFolderIsALink`). Media is a link only inside the BUILD's own folder (content/Media points at the course's Media, a real folder of the course), so every reader sees a changed picture where it really is.

The clock guard holds only while the build is still dated later than now. Anything changed while the clock reads earlier than the build's date (a page edited, deleted or renamed), and deployed after real time has passed that date, is sent as last built by every reader: no time a reader can see is later than the build's. A deploy, or Deploy pressed, while the build is still dated ahead rebuilds and closes the window. A fingerprint that needs no clock is a later piece (a digest of every entry's path, size and times, which four readers would have to compute identically).

On Windows a file overwritten in place and given back its old modification time is not seen (`knownLimitOn`): the creation time is read there in place of Windows' change time, which every build changes for the course's pictures by hard-linking them (`rejected`). A reader on Windows skips that case by name and says so.
A deploy typed at a command line for a section that has never been built still refuses (`typedByHand`).

On Netlify and Cloudflare a build deploy.py makes for a new address writes no trail line on a Mac: it runs in the website builder, which cannot reach the trail. deploy.sh asks the preview's site, the toolchain, the pages and the clock before it, so on a Mac deploy.py's own builds for those are a backstop that should not fire.
reuseTheLastBuild.measured: The cost of the question, nothing changed so every entry is read (the worst case). SPH3U's example course (320 files) copied 1, 10 and 60 times, warm, APFS, Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.6: see documentation/05-build-pipeline.md -> 'A deploy asks for itself whether anything changed (#768)' for the numbers, inside the website builder too.
reuseTheLastBuild.readers: Four readers answer the pages half and each runs every case: toolchain_paths.why_build_before_deploying (deploy.py, and Windows' deploy.ps1; it reads the stamp too), deploy.sh's pages_or_clock_ask_for_a_build with its site_was_built_by_this_toolchain (scripts/test_build_freshness_reuse.py), BuildFreshness.whyRebuild in each app, and the scheduled deploy's shell (ScheduledDeploy.oneShotCommand on the mac). The apps' readers do not read the stamp (builtWithToolchain.note) and take `inTheApps` where a case gives it. A preview's build is `previewBuild`, which every reader asks as well; one case here (only ever previewed) pins that it is asked BEFORE the toolchain. A new address is deploy.py's own question (Netlify and Cloudflare) and is not repeated here.

reasons.pages: Something in the course, a folder, or the course folder itself changed after the build that made the site started.
reasons.preview: The site is a preview's build (`previewBuild`). Asked first by every reader, before the toolchain, since #768's review: a preview never stamps its site.
reasons.toolchain: The launchers only: the site's stamp is missing or names another toolchain (`builtWithToolchain`).

rejected: Files only, as the plan first had it: misses a deleted page, a renamed one and a replaced attachment (measured by the plan's review on APFS), which is #741.

The modification time alone: misses a file overwritten in place with its old time kept, which a sync service does. Measured by the plan's review: every reader of modification times missed it, folders included.
Windows' own change time in place of its creation time: a build there hard-links the course's Media into its build folder, which changes each picture's change time, so every deploy would build again.
`-not -path '*/.*'`, the scheduled shell's form until #768: it matches the WHOLE path, so in a working folder kept under a hidden folder every file was skipped and the answer was always reuse.
An environment variable from the app saying the pages had been checked (the issue's first idea): a deploy typed by hand has no app to set it.
Asking the website builder (docker exec python3) from deploy.sh: a folder deploy need not start it at all, and the question costs milliseconds on the host.
A fingerprint of every file's bytes: exact, but it reads every picture on every deploy, and the apps and the scheduled shell compare times.
reuseTheLastBuild.rule: A deploy reuses the last build of a section exactly when that build is there, is not a preview's, was made by this toolchain, is not dated later than now, and nothing in the course (the course folder itself, its folders and files, hidden entries aside) was modified or changed after the build that made it STARTED; and, for Netlify and Cloudflare, the build carries the destination's address. Otherwise it builds again, once, then deploys. Every way of deploying asks: Deploy in the app, a deploy set for later, and deploy.sh, deploy.ps1 or deploy.bat typed at a command line.
reuseTheLastBuild.why: Russell's ruling, 2026-11-12 (#768): a deploy typed at the command line may reuse the last build, and the mac mirrors it, so the rule is one for both platforms and every way of deploying. Until then only the apps asked about the pages: a deploy.sh typed after an edit sent the last build and reported success, and a page deleted from the course stayed on the site (#741). Windows' deploy.py looked for the build in a folder Windows does not use, so every Netlify and Cloudflare deploy there rebuilt (55 to 66 s on a Lenovo 20QES70500); the path fix alone would have copied the mac's fault to Windows.

rules.when: the built site is older than the teacher's newest content
the built site was made by a PREVIEW
rules.why: **The one that is not obvious.** Serve mode bakes a live-reload client pointed at ws://localhost into every page. Publishing that makes visitors' browsers ask about 'access to other apps and services on this device' — so a preview build is never deploy-fresh, however recent it is. Detected by ANY built page containing the signature — `previewBuild`, which every checker reads (issue #136; the front page alone until then).

rules.when: the built site is newer than the content and was not built by a preview
the built index cannot be read
something was saved AFTER the build that made the site started, even though the built site is newer
rules.why: Issue #265. A build reads the settings and the pages when it starts and writes index.html minutes later, so a Save made while a publish was building is OLDER than index.html. Compared with index.html alone it looked built: the next Publish sent the same old site, said it had succeeded, and settingsSavedWhilePublishing told the teacher to do exactly that. So the time compared with is the START of the build that made the site on disk — read from buildStartedMarker when it is there, and the earlier of it and index.html's time when both are (an earlier time only ever costs a rebuild that was not needed; a later one sends a stale site). With no marker (a site built before this existed) index.html's time is used, as before. Rejected: comparing the build's copy of course_config.json with the course's (the plan review's A3) — the build copies the settings some seconds AFTER it reads them, so a Save in between matches the copy and is still missed, and it would not catch a PAGE saved during the build, which this does.

buildFreshness.theLaunchersMustDoThisToo: These rules were implemented in the APPS only, and that left a hole for two years' worth of command-line use. `deploy.py` refuses a preview build for the Netlify and Cloudflare destinations, but publishing TO A FOLDER is handled entirely host-side by `deploy.sh` / `deploy.ps1` — it never enters the container, so `deploy.py` never runs. From the command line, `./preview.sh CODE N` followed by `./deploy.sh CODE N --to-folder …` therefore published the live-reload client: measured 2026-09-05 as 230 of 244 files. The apps were never exposed, because BuildFreshness forces a rebuild first, which is why three destinations tested clean in August. That held for a whole preview's build, whose front page carries the client too; the MIXED state in (1) below reached the apps until issue #136, because they read the front page alone. They now read the same tree as the launchers — `previewBuild`. Both launchers now make the same check and rebuild. THREE things are needed, and each was discovered by getting it wrong. (1) The CHECK must read every HTML page, not just index.html: serve mode bakes the client into all of them and the tree is replaced file by file, so a clean front page in front of stale preview pages is a real state that front-page detection cannot see and publishes untouched. (2) The rebuild must STOP a preview that is still serving that section: the preview's sync watcher mirrors the serve build to the host every second and overwrites the rebuild within a second of it finishing. This was first blamed on bind-mount lag, which was wrong — a rebuild takes about 3 seconds and the tree is clean the moment it returns; the cause was always the race. (3) The WAIT after the rebuild must also cover every HTML page, for the same reason as (1). And (4), since #768: the launchers ask whether anything in the course CHANGED since the build, the question only the apps asked until then (`reuseTheLastBuild`), so a deploy typed after an edit, or after a page was deleted (#741), builds first.

credentialPrompts.everyRequestNote: An account ID is not a secret and is shown as it is typed; a token is, and is not. Getting that backwards either puts a live credential on a screen a class can see, or hides a code the teacher needs to check they pasted correctly.
credentialPrompts.expiryAdviceIsLoadBearing: Both token steps tell the teacher to set an expiry past the end of the school year. Netlify's box starts at 7 DAYS, and an expired token does not announce itself - publishing simply stops working weeks later, which is diagnosed as the app breaking. Cloudflare's TTL is the same trap. The Cloudflare steps also require choosing 'Include' and the teacher's own account under 'Account Resources': a token that names no account cannot publish, and what comes back does not mention accounts at all.
credentialPrompts.matchedOnWordsNotWholeLine: The two launchers word these prompts slightly differently and are free to keep doing so, so the match is on the words that NAME the credential — 'netlify token', 'cloudflare token', 'cloudflare account id' — not on the whole line.
credentialPrompts.note: Which launcher prompt is a request for a publishing credential, and which one it is. Authored rather than read out of the code, because this is the half that must fail when the matching changes: a prompt that stops being recognised does not crash anything — the teacher simply gets the old one-line question back and no way to answer it.
credentialPrompts.theHelpVariantIsNeverMatched: cloudflareAccountIDHelp carries the SAME steps and link as cloudflareAccountID and differs only in why it is asking, so it must never be returned by the prompt matching: it is opened by a teacher pressing a button beside the Account ID field in Course Settings or the new-course wizard, possibly before any token exists, so it must not talk about 'the token you just made'. credentialPrompts.whyNoBrowserOpens: The launchers used to run `open` (macOS) or `Start-Process` (Windows) on the token page the moment they asked, so a browser tab appeared unasked while the teacher was looking at the app. Reported as disconcerting: an application that takes over the screen reads as something going wrong, not as help. credentialRequests.note: What a teacher reads when a first deploy stops to ask for a Netlify or Cloudflare credential. cases.why: The flag goes straight after the course and section, before the destination, so every shape of deploy carries it in the same place. Only a SCHEDULED deploy passes it: pressing Deploy runs the launcher through a pseudo-terminal, so a question from the publishing step comes back to the app and becomes a dialog the teacher answers — that is the feature, not a fault, and it must keep working.

cases.name: A scheduled Cloudflare deploy carries the flag and the destination
A scheduled folder deploy carries it too
cases.why: A folder deploy asks nothing today — it never reaches a web host and never names a site — so the flag changes nothing here. It is passed anyway because it describes the CALLER, not the destination: it says nobody is at the computer, and that stays true if a question is ever added to this path.

deployArguments.note: Given a course's configuration, what deploy.sh is asked to do. One place must decide this in each app — on the mac it is DeployCommand.arguments, shared by the Deploy button, the assistant and the scheduled-deploy alarm. Built separately anywhere and this happens: the assistant path never passed --target cloudflare, and a Cloudflare course deployed to Netlify. Nothing failed; the site simply appeared on the wrong host. Every destination is NAMED, Netlify included (--target netlify) since #668: a deploy.sh given no destination now reads the course's saved destinations itself (Russell, 2026-11-01), so a call from the app must say which leg it is. A course can configure more than one destination now (additional_deploy_targets, in file-formats.json) — Deploy walks them in order and calls this same argument-building logic once per destination, so every case above still applies per leg; there is no separate multi-destination argument shape to test. A case may carry `unattended: true`, which is what the SCHEDULED deploy passes and nothing else does — the Deploy button, the assistant and an MCP client all leave it off. It adds `--non-interactive`, which tells the launcher that any question a teacher would have to answer must become a refusal rather than a prompt nobody can answer or a default nobody chose. What it refuses, on both platforms, is launcherFlags.nonInteractive.

helperBootstrap.rule: The Mac app carries Apple-silicon copies of Colima, Lima, the Docker CLI and Buildx, and the website builder's starting disk, in Contents/Resources/helpers with a MANIFEST, and tells a launcher where through PLANTOIR_BUNDLED_HELPERS (set by HelperPrograms.environment only when the folder exists, so every run the app starts carries it, scheduled publishes included). The launchers INSTALL the programs into Plantoir's tools folder and run them from there, never from inside the app: copied (cloned) and checked against the MANIFEST when the app's copy is usable, downloaded and checked against the pinned SHA-256s otherwise. A program found outside Plantoir's folder is used as it is. The stamp (.installed) is read as three questions about Plantoir's own copies only — different pins, damaged bytes, or no stamp at all — and a missing stamp means replace only when the app has a copy to replace them with. Buildx is installed only when `docker buildx version` fails, outside the stamp, and a link is never replaced. On a first start the website builder is created from the app's starting disk with --disk-image; any failure is retried once with the same size and no disk image, which downloads it as before.

stamp.manifest: Contents/Resources/helpers/MANIFEST: arch <arm64>, the same pins line, image vm/<name>, then one <sha256>  <path> line for every file but the starting disk, which Colima checks itself. Written by mac-app/Vendor/fetch-helpers.sh and written again by publish.sh after it signs the programs.
stamp.shape: the pins line (pins <colima> <lima> <docker> <buildx> <starting disk SHA-512>), then one source <program> <bundled|downloaded> line per program it vouches for (per program since the implementation review's L5: one install can replace one program and leave the others as an earlier install set them up), then one <sha256>  <path> line per program file it vouches for (bin/colima, bin/limactl, bin/lima, bin/docker). A program of Plantoir's with no line is UNRECORDED, not damaged (L6).

nonInteractive.note: What `--non-interactive` must refuse, on BOTH platforms. The list is the point: a flag that refuses in six places on one platform and four on the other is a scheduled publish that hangs on one of them. deploy.py is shared Python, so those refusals cannot drift; the launcher's own are per-platform and are written out here so the second one is copied rather than invented. The course-code guard is refused as of 2026-09-09; it is the FIRST entry below, and the entry carries what was rejected and why.

refusals.bothLaunchers: deploy.sh AND preview.sh, and the second is the one that is easy to miss. A scheduled publish BUILDS before it publishes, and the mac's launchd agent runs preview.sh --build-only directly. preview.sh has no `set -e`, so without the flag its read fails at end of input, `${_ans:-Y}` takes the DEFAULT, and the build retargets a DIFFERENT course code — which then publishes successfully against the wrong course. That is a worse failure than a refusal, because nothing looks wrong.
refusals.question: Fix course code to '<CODE>'? [Y/n] — the guard for a code ending in a digit zero
refusals.reachedWhen: The course code matches three letters, a digit and a zero. DECIDED by Russell 2026-09-09 to refuse; it was deliberately unchanged before that, and the reasoning both ways is kept below because it was measured rather than guessed.
refusals.refuse: Say which question could not be asked, and that publishing or previewing this section once from Plantoir sorts it out.
refusals.rejected: KEEPING THE CODE AS TYPED, which was the other defensible answer and is recorded so it is not re-proposed as new: by the time a schedule exists the code came from course_config.json rather than a keyboard, so there is no typo to fix, and a genuinely wrong code still fails loudly at "Course folder not found". It was rejected because a silent retarget on the build leg is indistinguishable from success, and because a refusal that names the question is consistent with every other question under this flag. The cost is real and worth stating: a teacher whose course code is hand-typed in that shape — ENG10, MAT10 — cannot publish unattended until the code is changed.
refusals.whatHappenedBefore: TWO different unattended failures, one per launcher, and a scheduled publish meets both because it builds before it publishes. `preview.sh` has no `set -e`: the read fails at end of input, the answer variable stays empty, the [Y/n] DEFAULT is taken, and the build retargets a DIFFERENT course code — announcing it with “Using corrected course code”, which nobody is there to read. `deploy.sh` has `set -euo pipefail`: the same failed read ends the script on the spot with exit 1. Measured: it prints the guard's two explanatory lines (“It looks like you entered 'ICS30'…”) and then stops — no prompt text, no error, no reason. So the shape today is “builds the wrong course, then stops mid-sentence”.
refusals.whoItReaches: MEASURED 2026-09-06, and it is narrower than the first draft of this entry claimed. The guard matches three letters, a digit and a zero — and NO code in either catalogue the wizard offers matches it: 0 of 1930 Ontario codes and 0 of 117 British Columbia codes (BC codes are MFMP-10 / MPREC11 shaped). A course code is free text up to twelve characters (CourseCodeRule), so it is still reachable — but only by a code a teacher typed freehand, which is exactly the case the guard was written for. That cuts BOTH ways in the decision below: refusing breaks far fewer real courses than feared, and the whole prompt is rarer than it looks.

refusals.question: Continue anyway? [y/N] — the warning when a section is not listed in course_config.json
refusals.reachedWhen: preview.ps1 is asked to build a section the course's configuration does not list. WINDOWS ONLY, and not drift: preview.sh has exactly one read prompt (its course-code guard) and simply does not ask this. Added from Windows 2026-09-09; launcherFlags is authored rather than generated, so that side could record it without asking the mac.
refusals.refuse: Say which question could not be asked, and that adding this section to the course in Plantoir — or previewing it once by hand — answers it.
refusals.whatHappenedBefore: Its default is NO, so an unattended build of an unlisted section printed "Cancelled." and exited 1 to a console nobody was watching. Measured on PowerShell 5.1.26100: under the scheduled wrapper's `powershell -NonInteractive` an unanswered Read-Host does not return an empty string at all — it THROWS PSInvalidOperationException, and preview.ps1's own $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' kills the script before the default is ever consulted. Either way the publish does not happen and nothing says why.

refusals.question: Paste Netlify token
refusals.reachedWhen: Netlify is not connected on this computer.
refusals.refuse: Say Netlify is not connected, that connecting asks for a token nobody is here to paste, and that publishing this section once from Plantoir sorts it out.

refusals.question: Paste Cloudflare token
refusals.reachedWhen: Cloudflare is not connected on this computer.

refusals.question: Paste Cloudflare Account ID
refusals.reachedWhen: Cloudflare is the destination, the app passed no --account, the token cannot list its own account, and nothing was remembered.
refusals.refuse: Say the Account ID is not saved, and to add it in Plantoir ▸ Settings ▸ Deploying, then deploy again (#490: the ID is the teacher's, kept in Settings since #457/#491, not in a course's settings) — the same place the app already names when it refuses to SCHEDULE for this reason ('…then schedule this again'; on Windows the app's own sentences say File ▸ Settings ▸ Deploying, where the item is there).

refusals.question: (not a question) a saved credential that fails its check
refusals.reachedWhen: The saved token does not validate.
refusals.refuse: Refuse, and LEAVE THE TOKEN IN PLACE rather than clearing it. The check is a network call, so “this computer was offline at 6am” and “the token was revoked” look identical from there — and throwing away a working credential only a person can replace is the more expensive of the two mistakes. An ordinary publish still clears it, with somebody there to paste a new one.

refusals.question: Enter Netlify site name
refusals.reachedWhen: There is no Netlify site for this section — either it has never been published, or the site was deleted at Netlify since the alarm was set and the lookup comes back 404.
refusals.refuse: Refuse. The address is what students type, it is global to all of Netlify, and it cannot be changed later without every existing link breaking, so there is no safe default. This is the state that hung for 45 minutes on Windows.

refusals.question: First time setup... what is your last name?
refusals.reachedWhen: A new Cloudflare project is being named and no surname is saved on this computer.
refusals.refuse: Refuse. On the Netlify path this is unreachable — naming the site is refused first. Note the asymmetry: with a surname already saved, a new Cloudflare project asks NOTHING (the address is derived from the course, section, year and surname), so nothing is refused there.

refusals.question: Choose a username for these unit plans
refusals.reachedWhen: A protected share of a course's unit plans (deploy.sh <CODE> --plans --protect, or a sticky one) with no username and password saved for the course, or with --change-password.
refusals.refuse: Say nobody is here to choose them, and that sharing the plans once from Plantoir, where they can be chosen, sorts it out. The password question after it is never reached.

refusals.question: any other prompt
refusals.reachedWhen: A question is added upstream that this list does not name.
refusals.refuse: The prompt helper itself refuses when the flag is set, naming the question verbatim. A backstop, so a new question fails loudly instead of being answered with a default nobody chose.

launcherFlags.note: What the APP passes the launchers, beyond the deploy arguments already above. Both platforms drive their own launcher — `preview.sh` here, `preview.ps1` there — and those scripts must accept the same flags, because the apps are written against the same behaviour. A flag renamed in one script and not the other fails at the worst moment: the launcher prints 'Unknown option' and exits, and to a teacher that is a preview that just did not start.

preview.meaning: Build the section's site and STOP. Do not serve it, do not take a port.
usedFor: the assistant's rebuild when no window is open
the build a deploy does first when the built site is stale
preview.why: Serving is the section window's job — it holds the port lease and the web view. A second server started behind its back would take a port the window then could not have.

preview.meaning: Only with --build-only (alone it is refused: "❌ --for-deploy goes with --build-only.", exit 1). Changes nothing the build does: it names this build in the process table as a deploy's first step, so the other launchers' guards can tell it from a rebuild.
usedFor: the build a deploy does first when the built site is stale
notUsedFor: the assistant's rebuild, which is a build and not a deploy
the build leg of a deploy set for later, whose own script is already in the table and counts as one
deploy.sh's own rebuild, which the deploy.sh that started it already names
preview.why: GitHub #729, measured in #706's reproduction: the window's or an assistant's deploy builds with preview.sh --build-only BEFORE its deploy.sh starts, and that line was the same as the assistant's rebuild, so during the build leg another program's deploy of the section was not refused and its build broke the first. With the flag, shared-rules.json -> deployWhileItsSectionDeploys says 'already being deployed' for the build leg and 'already being built' for a rebuild, and previewWhileItsSectionDeploys refuses a preview during the build leg. An argument rather than an environment variable, because `ps -Ao args` shows arguments only.

preview.meaning: Serve on this host port. The websocket goes on port + 1000.
preview.why: The app leases the port, not the script — several previews run at once, one per section, and the app is the only thing that knows which are taken.

preview.meaning: Kill this section's container-side processes and exit. Start nothing.
preview.why: Ending the host-side script leaves the build or server running INSIDE the container. Stop mode reclaims them, and it finds them by working directory — so it catches a running BUILD as well as a server, which is why a stop that has not finished will kill a rebuild that has just started.

preview.meaning: Refuse rather than ask. preview.sh asks one question — the 'Open' course-code guard — and under this flag it says which question it could not ask and exits 3, the same code deploy.sh and deploy.py use for it.
usedFor: the BUILD leg of a publish set to happen on its own
the rebuild deploy.sh does when a preview-built site would otherwise be published
preview.why: preview.sh needs this even though it publishes nothing, and the reason is the failure it prevents rather than tidiness. It has no `set -e`: unattended, the guard's read fails at end of input, `${_ans:-Y}` takes the DEFAULT, and the build quietly retargets a DIFFERENT course code — which the deploy then publishes successfully, against the wrong course. Nothing looks wrong. A refusal is the better failure. Two callers pass it: the mac's launchd wrapper runs preview.sh directly for the build leg, and deploy.sh forwards it to its own rebuild.

setup.meaning: Use this image instead of the one the recipe hash names.
setup.why: Testing a locally built image. `verify.sh` uses it; the apps never do.
For a machine with several (desktop-linux, colima, default).

setup.meaning: Everything after a literal `--` is forwarded to `setup_course.py`.
usedFor: pre-populating a new course: the mac passes `-- --install-example`
setup.why: The launcher owns the container and the Python owns the questions, so anything that is a question for the Python is passed through rather than re-parsed.

Checked 2026-08-16 rather than assumed, because the two calls looking different is exactly the kind of thing that turns out to be a silent bug. Pass the separator: it is the documented form in both launchers' help, and it keeps working if either ever starts rejecting unknown flags the way `preview.sh` already does.

The mac's launchers read the variable since GitHub #664, and Windows' preview.ps1 and deploy.ps1 since #682 (Write-TrailLine, run against every case by windows-app/test_launcher_rules.ps1 section 6). On Windows an absolute folder means a drive letter and a separator, or a UNC \\server\share: [IO.Path]::IsPathRooted is true on PowerShell 5.1 for \state\Logs and C:state, which are relative to the current drive or folder.

launcherTrailFolder.note: Where a launcher writes its own lines on the breadcrumb trail (a refusal, or the launcher's own lines from a publish it runs - on Windows Task Scheduler runs deploy.ps1; on the Mac the app runs a scheduled publish itself, so those lines are the app's). The app hands over its trail folder in this variable, and a launcher takes it only when it is an absolute path.

rejected.option: Set the variable only when the app runs with --state-dir.
rejected.why: The unit suite's integration tests run real launchers from a test host whose own trail is a throwaway folder and which has no --state-dir, so their refusal lines would still land in the real trail. It would also need a second branch to REMOVE a stale value inherited from whatever started the app. Setting it always costs nothing in the plain app, where the value is the folder the launcher would have computed anyway.

rejected.option: Hand the launcher a redirected HOME instead.
rejected.why: HOME also decides the builds root and where the helper programs live, which --state-dir deliberately keeps real (#154, #641): a UI test builds into the real builds root and cleans it up. Only the trail moves.

rejected.option: Accept a relative value, resolved against the working folder.
rejected.why: A stray relative value would start a trail inside the teacher's working folder, beside their courses. Nothing that sets the variable on purpose has any reason to hand over anything but a full path.

launcherTrailFolder.rule: A launcher writes its trail lines into the folder named by the variable when it is an absolute path, without a trailing separator, and into its own default folder otherwise. It moves the trail ONLY: the builds root, the helper programs and everything else still follow the home folder. The app sets the variable in EVERY launcher's environment, to its own trail folder, overriding any value it inherited.

browserSafe.note: The address handed to the teacher's browser. Safari tries IPv6 (::1) first for 'localhost' and the container only publishes the port on IPv4, which reads to a teacher as 'the server dropped the connection'. The numeric address sidesteps it entirely. Check whether your default browser has the same behaviour before deciding this is mac-only.

modelTiers.note: What must be TRUE of the local assistant's model choice on both platforms. The numbers are NOT shared — a threshold measured on one machine says nothing about another's — with one exception, named below: the request cap, which is a value both apps put on the wire rather than a measurement of anybody's hardware. But the shape is, and so is every word a teacher sees.

requirements.detail: A smaller assistant and a larger one. Not one, not four.
requirements.why: One rung means either the weakest machine cannot run it or the strongest is wasted. Four means four ladders to re-measure whenever a model, quant or context size changes.

requirements.detail: Read the machine's memory (and whatever else your platform can see) and pick.
requirements.rule: The rung is CHOSEN from the hardware, never asked
requirements.why: A teacher cannot answer 'how much memory does this need?' and should not be asked to. The mac reads physical memory and decides.

requirements.detail: The interface says exactly these, and nothing else.
requirements.rule: The teacher never learns the model's name
requirements.why: A download sheet reading 'Plantoir picked Qwen3 4B to suit this Mac's memory' tells a teacher nothing they can act on and quite a lot about plumbing they never asked about. The real model lives in the filename and the download URL, which are never shown. A mac test fails if a model name, parameter count or file format reaches that string.

requirements.detail: Never inside the container that builds the site.
requirements.rule: The model runs on the HOST, with hardware acceleration
requirements.why: Measured on an M4 Pro, same model and same 3,411-token prompt: 175 seconds inside Colima against 2.1 seconds natively on Metal, and 5.5 tokens/second against 158. That is the largest single number in the feature. See documentation/12-windows-app.md for what to use on Windows.

requirements.detail: Re-run the routing suite when the model, quant or context size changes.
requirements.rule: A model that inverts polarity is VETOED, whatever it scores
requirements.why: An inversion publishes a page the teacher asked to hide — the one failure that reports success. Two 3B-class models were rejected on this alone: Qwen2.5 3B inverted 9 trials in 10, Llama-3.2 3B 10 in 10, on the same sentence.

requirements.detail: Every request to the local engine carries max_tokens 512.
requirements.rule: Every request caps how much the model may write
requirements.why: Uncapped, a reply is bounded only by the context. Measured on an M4 Pro with the smaller assistant (llama.cpp b10435 on Metal, Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M, context 8192): one ordinary request — publish tomorrow's class and every page it links to — produced 5,435 tokens of a page list in 42 seconds, three trials in three, and what arrived was unusable. 2,757 prompt plus 5,435 written is 8,192 exactly, so the context was the only thing stopping it. On the larger assistant the same shape would run about 216 seconds at that tier's measured 63.2 tokens a second, past the mac client's own 180-second timeout, so it would fail rather than answer. The NUMBER is shared even though the numbers around it are not: it is not a measurement of one machine, it is a value both apps put on the wire, like the preview ports, and two apps sending different caps is a difference no test on either side could see. 512 was measured against this surface's own tokenizer — an ordinary tool call is 16 to 60 tokens, twenty page titles 203, twenty-four long real-world titles 384, fifty-eight short titles 545 — so the only legitimate shape it cuts is an explicit list of about fifty-five or more classes, and publish_pages already takes onOrAfter and before, which asks for any number of classes in about sixty. ONE SHAPE DOES NOT FIT, and it has now been measured: a second lap echoing back the relative PATHS list_pages hands over - up to sixty of them, and far longer per item than a class title. Sixty real paths from a 257-page course are 975 tokens against this model's tokenizer, so such a call crosses 512 at about the thirty-first path (the twenty-sixth for a section's longest). The risk is real, bounded and named. What keeps it off a teacher's screen is that the model does not write that call: primed with the list_pages result carrying all sixty paths and asked to publish all of them, the smaller assistant answered with a range - pages: all - in 35 completion tokens, three trials of three, finishing naturally - one model, one phrasing, worth that much and no more. Re-measured 2026-09-26 for #197 on six example payloads, it answered pages: all in none of 108 cells - every one an invented list cut off at this cap, which is refused - and pages: all itself, which the app used to answer 'Nothing needed changing.', is refused in code since then with wording.everyPageIsNotAPageToPublish (assist-cases.json -> pagesNamingNoPage). A teacher who does meet it is told wording.answerWasCutOff, whose advice - fewer pages at a time - is followable in precisely this case. Sizing the cap to the worst imaginable call is a cap that never fires, which is the state this rule exists to prevent. Measured 2026-09-19; conditions in research/ai-assist/token-cap-results.txt.

requirements.detail: Whether or not its half-written arguments happen to parse, and whether or not it had got as far as naming a tool. Nothing runs, and the teacher is answered with wording.answerWasCutOff - and the whole TURN is wound back out of the conversation sent to the model, the half-written reply and the teacher's sentence together, so the retry that wording asks for is not sent with the request that ran away still in front of it. Two boundaries: what the teacher SEES is not wound back (their sentence stays in the transcript), and neither is a turn that failed because the engine could not be reached or timed out - that one reports an engine failure rather than asking for a rephrase.
requirements.rule: A reply the engine stopped part way runs no tool and says so
requirements.why: A separate rule from the cap, and needed BECAUSE of it: a cap turns a rare context overrun into a routine stopping point, so what the app does with a stopped reply matters more after capping than before. Parsing cannot be the check. Measured on an M4 Pro (llama.cpp b10435, Qwen2.5-1.5B Q4_K_M) by sweeping the cap across every cut point of two ordinary requests: llama.cpp closes the arguments object before the tool-call wrapper, so at max_tokens 28 a stopped deploy_section call parsed cleanly as {course, section}, and at 42 a stopped publish_pages call parsed as a page list one title long where the teacher had named more. Cut earlier still, at 8, the tool name had not been written yet and a raw tool-call fragment arrived in the message CONTENT, which an app that shows content verbatim would print in front of a teacher. And a tool that takes no arguments at all, like undo_last_change, is readable however early it was cut, so a parse check would simply run it. The reason the turn ended is the only signal that tells a finished answer from a fragment.

requirements.detail: A reply that finished normally and named a tool but wrote NO arguments for it - nothing, only whitespace, or an object with no keys - runs only when the section window can supply everything the tool needs. The window supplies course and section. A tool needs more than that when its schema REQUIRES any other argument (a date, a page, a time), or when it changes pages (readOnly false) and its schema declares any other argument at all (which pages, which dates, which unit) - a write told only its section has nothing to act on. Otherwise it runs: undo (no arguments), rebuilding the preview, the deploy (still behind its own button), and a read whose other argument only narrows it. Refused, nothing runs, and the teacher is answered with wording.answerLeftOutWhatItWasFor - NOT wording.answerWasCutOff, whose advice is about the teacher's request - and the trail says the assistant wrote nothing for that tool. A schema with NO required key (undo_last_change's has none) requires nothing, the same as an empty list; each case's required, properties and readOnly are the tool's own. Written arguments of any kind are readable, however little they say - binding the window's course and section, and the tool's own refusals, decide what happens next.
requirements.rule: A finished reply that wrote nothing runs a tool only when the window supplies everything that tool needs
requirements.why: Issue #198, 2026-09-23. An empty string is readable on purpose, because undo_last_change takes nothing and llama.cpp sends an empty string for it, so a gate refusing every empty call would refuse 'Undo that', the tool a card reaches most. But the same yes let a finished reply naming publish_pages with nothing written reach the tool, where, bound to the window's section with no pages and no dates, it answered that nothing had been named to change - a sentence reading as a complaint about the teacher's request, when the teacher had named pages and the model had dropped them. Measured against the recorded routing runs (990 tool-call rows in research/ai-assist): 175 empty-argument calls, every one to a tool that requires nothing, none to a tool that needs a course or section - so this costs nothing measured. REJECTED: refusing every empty call (breaks undo); refusing every tool with a required list - the first cut of this rule - which refused 'rebuild the preview' and the deploy on an empty call although the window supplies everything they take (found on review); and 'readable when every REQUIRED argument is one the window supplies' alone, which keeps the empty publish_pages running because its real content is optional in its schema.

agents.couldNotStart: Plantoir couldn’t start a Claude session for {course}. If Claude Code was updated or moved recently, restarting Plantoir may be enough.
agents.handover: a configuration file written for this one session and named after the course
agents.isolationNote: --strict-mcp-config means only the server in that file is loaded, so a teacher's own MCP servers are neither used nor disturbed.
agents.serverEnvironmentWhy: Written as "env" beside "args" in mcp-{course}.json, so the server holds an assist lease on the course the door was opened from (shared-rules.json -> doorCourseHold). Windows since #430, the mac since #458. The argv stays the folder alone (serverArguments).
agents.writesNothingElse: Both files are in the app's own data directory. Nothing is written into the teacher's working folder, and nothing global is touched.

agents.argumentsNote: Six dotted -c overrides (the fifth names the course to the server's environment, and since #783 the sixth names the door, serverEnvironment) and the greeting as a positional first message. No sandbox flag and no approval flag: Codex asks the teacher itself before any tool that changes a page, and passing a flag would quietly widen permissions they set for themselves. Dotted keys rather than one inline table because they merge into a teacher's configuration one key at a time and match the published documentation.
agents.couldNotStart: Plantoir couldn’t start a Codex session for {course}. If Codex was updated or moved recently, restarting Plantoir may be enough.
agents.handover: inline configuration on the command line, so nothing at all is written for the connection
agents.isolationNote: Codex has no equivalent of --strict-mcp-config, and the command-line layer is MERGED with the teacher's own configuration rather than replacing it, so their own MCP servers load beside Plantoir's. This is structural rather than an omission in the documentation and cannot be fixed from Plantoir's side.
agents.scriptNameCarriesTheAgentWhy: The second door's script is named after the agent as well as the course. The script is read by the terminal AFTER Plantoir has handed it over, so two doors sharing one name would let a second launch seconds later reach the first window with the wrong command line - which is the same race the per-course naming already exists to stop.
agents.serverEnvironmentWhy: Passed as a fifth override, -c mcp_servers.plantoir.env.PLANTOIR_DOOR_COURSE="{course}" (escaped for TOML, then for the shell, like every value), so the server holds an assist lease on the course the door was opened from, exactly as the Claude door's env does (shared-rules.json -> doorCourseHold.whichDoors). The mac since #458 (Russell, 2026-10-07: both doors); Windows since #468 (2026-10-08, CodexLauncher.Arguments). Codex 0.155.1 reads the form: measured with codex mcp get --json.
agents.timeoutsAreOverriddenWhy: Codex's own defaults are version-dependent - 30s startup and 300s per tool in its current source, 10s and 60s in its published reference - and both tool figures are too short, because a publish is awaited and a first one builds the image and uploads, which takes minutes. 60s and 1800s are passed rather than trusted.
agents.valuesAreEscapedTwice: Each value sits inside a TOML basic string inside a shell-single-quoted argument, so it is escaped for TOML first (backslash, double quote and control characters) and for the shell second. Getting the inner layer wrong fails QUIETLY: an unparseable value is not rejected, it is treated as a raw string, so args stops being a list and the door greets the teacher and then cannot start its server.
agents.writesNothingElse: No configuration file exists for this door: the server is described in the arguments. Nothing is written into the teacher's working folder, and nothing is added to or read from their own Codex configuration.

agents.argumentsNote: The connection file after @ (an ABSOLUTE path: a relative one is read against Copilot's own folder), GitHub's own servers turned off, and the greeting sent as the first turn of an interactive session (-i). No permission flag of any kind (Russell, 2026-11-13): no --allow-tool, --deny-tool, --allow-all-*, --no-ask-user or --yolo. Copilot asks the teacher in its own window before each Plantoir tool that changes something, before each command a printable handout needs (tectonic, pdftoppm, mkdir), and before deploying, as the other two doors do; the teacher can answer that it need not ask again in this folder. What Plantoir cannot see, and so cannot promise: a teacher's or a school's own Copilot settings can let it act without asking - an approval saved earlier (~/.copilot/permissions-config.json), defaultPermissionMode allow-all, COPILOT_ALLOW_ALL=true, or an organisation's 'assisted' mode, whose judge reads each tool's hints (deploy_section's destructiveHint is false). The same is true of Codex's 'Always allow'. No -C: the script's own cd sets the folder, and -C arrived only in 1.0.42 (flagsWhy).
agents.connectionFileWhy: A file, written with a JSON writer and never by joining strings, rather than the inline JSON form --additional-mcp-config also takes: the inline form puts a string full of double quotes inside a shell argument on the mac and inside cmd /k quoting for npm's copilot.cmd on Windows, where #736 already spent a release on quoting. Its own name, mcp-{course}-copilot.json, and not Claude's mcp-{course}.json, for the reason scriptNameCarriesTheAgentWhy gives. type 'local' is the form measured in the trial (2026-11-13, 38 of 38 tools worked); Copilot 1.0.108's schema calls it a legacy alias of 'stdio', which an older Copilot may not know. tools ['*'] is every tool. timeout is timeoutWhy.
agents.couldNotStart: Plantoir couldn’t start a GitHub Copilot session for {course}. If GitHub Copilot was updated or moved recently, restarting Plantoir may be enough.

flagsWhy.--additional-mcp-config: Adds Plantoir's server for this session only. It predates Copilot's oldest changelog entry (0.0.328). Copilot reads, in order, the teacher's ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json, the folder's .mcp.json or .github/mcp.json, plugins, then this flag, and the later one wins on a name, so Plantoir's 'plantoir' is the one used.
flagsWhy.--disable-builtin-mcps: Turns off GitHub's own repository server (github-mcp-server): tools about repositories and pull requests in every choice the model makes are how routing degrades, and a course session has no business acting on a teacher's repositories. It also predates the oldest changelog entry. Measured 2026-11-13 with copilot mcp list: with the flag github-mcp-server is listed 'disabled' and computer-use, a local plugin, is still listed, which is why --disable-mcp-server computer-use follows it.
flagsWhy.--disable-mcp-server computer-use: Turns off computer-use, GitHub's desktop-control server (a local plugin that takes screenshots and clicks; its plugin.json calls it in preview), which --disable-builtin-mcps leaves on: 1.0.108's own built-in list is github-mcp-server, WorkIQ, browser-use and github-copilot-browser. A course session has no use for it, and a teacher's or school's allow-all would remove its consent prompt. Measured 2026-11-13: with the flag, copilot mcp list shows computer-use (local, disabled); naming a server an older Copilot does not have exits 0, so it raises no version floor. It turns the server off for this session only: a teacher who wants it can still start Copilot on their own, and their own settings are not changed (review M2, taken by the director).
flagsWhy.-i: Starts an interactive session with the greeting already sent (-p is the one-shot form, which cannot ask the teacher anything).

agents.folderTrust: The first time Copilot is started in a folder it asks whether to trust it (Yes, Yes and remember, No; No ends the session). Plantoir does not answer it for the teacher, as it does not for Claude Code, which asks the same kind of question.
agents.handover: a configuration file written for this one session, named after the course and the agent

helpAnchors.why: The Help book's page ids (#839's outline, one anchor a page). Russell, 2026-11-13: wherever Plantoir offers GitHub Copilot to a teacher who does not have it, it links the github-education page. This door is shown only while Copilot is installed (hiddenWhenNotInstalled), so it offers Copilot to nobody who lacks it; the first such offer is #855's set-up item, which links github-education.

identity.rule: A copilot found on the search list (searchedForInOrder) is used only when it is GitHub's: either its path, links followed, lies inside an npm install of npmPackage (…/node_modules/@github/copilot/…), or it is a program signed with signedIdentifier and signedTeam under an Apple-issued certificate (requirement). Any other copilot is passed over and the search goes on down the list; none left means no door.
identity.requirement: identifier "copilot" and anchor apple generic and certificate leaf[subject.OU] = "VEKTX9H2N7"
identity.why: Homebrew's own copilot formula is a different vendor's program (Amazon's ECS and Fargate tool, deprecated but installable until 2027-07-06) and writes the same /opt/homebrew/bin/copilot as GitHub's cask copilot-cli (measured, brew info, 2026-11-13). Without this check a teacher who typed brew install copilot would be shown GitHub Copilot… and the door would open a program that stops at once on --additional-mcp-config. This checks which program it is, never whether anybody is signed in (neverProbedForSignIn still holds). #855 calls the same check after it installs Copilot.
identity.measured: 2026-11-13, this Mac (Apple silicon, macOS 26): codesign -dv on the cask's binary (1.0.105, which runs 1.0.108) gives Identifier=copilot, TeamIdentifier=VEKTX9H2N7. The check with the program's pages left unhashed (kSecCSDoNotValidateExecutable) took 6 to 10 ms on the 196 MB binary against 0.51 to 0.55 s for a full check, so it runs at launch and on activation with no cache; it refused an unsigned script, Claude Code's own signed program and /bin/ls. Measured by the implementation reviewer the same day: the binary in GitHub's install script's archive (releases/latest/download/copilot-darwin-arm64.tar.gz, the same file the cask fetches) is signed Identifier=copilot, Authority 'Developer ID Application: GitHub (VEKTX9H2N7)', and is accepted; /bin/ls re-signed ad hoc with identifier copilot is refused. What it proves: that the program started is GitHub's launcher. It does not prove every byte it runs is (the signed cask binary 1.0.105 runs the auto-updated, unsigned JavaScript package from ~/Library/Caches/copilot/pkg/…/1.0.108), and a GitHub binary altered after signing still passes, since its pages are not hashed. An npm install is a #!/usr/bin/env node script and needs node on the Terminal's PATH, as an npm Claude Code does.
identity.onWindows: Windows owes its own form of the same check (the windows issue for #783): Homebrew does not exist there, but any copilot.exe on PATH is not proof of GitHub's.

agents.isolationNote: Copilot has no equivalent of --strict-mcp-config: --additional-mcp-config ADDS to the teacher's own configuration, so their own MCP servers load beside Plantoir's, as with Codex. Copilot also reads the teacher's own instructions and personal skills (~/.agents/skills), as Claude Code reads ~/.claude; neither door can stop an assistant reading its owner's own set-up. A teacher who once turned Plantoir's server off in Copilot (/mcp disable plantoir, saved in disabledMcpServers) gets sessions with no Plantoir tools: --enable-mcp-server would turn it on for one run but arrived only in 1.0.80, so it is not passed, and Help names the case.
agents.measured: Copilot CLI 1.0.108 (Homebrew cask copilot-cli, auto-updated past the cask's 1.0.105), this Mac, 2026-11-13. The trial (copilot-trial/RESULTS.md, section 4) started it with this connection file shape and all 38 tools worked, named plantoir-{tool} and found through Copilot's own tool search; AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and the skills under .claude/skills and .agents/skills were read with no change. Measured here without starting a session: an unknown flag prints 'unexpected argument' and exits 1 in 0.07 s; copilot mcp list does NOT read --additional-mcp-config (it lists only the teacher's and the built-in servers), so the file was checked another way. The implementation review called Copilot's own reader (mcpConfigReadAndMergeAdditional in 1.0.108's runtime.node, with a scratch HOME, no session, no sign-in) on the file this door writes, for a folder holding a space, an apostrophe, a double quote and an accented letter: every key came back, timeout 1800000 included. A wrong top-level key, a missing command, a bad type, a string timeout and a missing file each throw, and the CLI then stops, which stoppedAtOnce explains. The one silent failure is a misspelt optional key (timeoutMs was dropped with no warning, leaving the 60 s default), so the whole written file is pinned to connectionFile by the mac's contract test. The schema's additionalProperties false is not enforced by that reader.
rejected: The inline JSON form of --additional-mcp-config (connectionFileWhy).
Sharing Claude's mcp-{course}.json: two doors launched seconds apart would rewrite the file the other's window has not yet read.
-C <folder> (added in 1.0.42): an older Copilot stops at once on it, and the script's cd does the same job.
--enable-mcp-server plantoir (1.0.80): raises the oldest version that works for one rare case (isolationNote).

--allow-all-mcp-server-instructions: it would include instructions from every server the teacher has, not only Plantoir's; the greeting and list_courses carry the same facts as Plantoir's instructions.
Pre-allowing Plantoir's read-only tools or the three handout commands: Russell, 2026-11-13, Plantoir passes no permissions.
A separate COPILOT_HOME, to keep the teacher's own servers and skills out: it would also hide their sign-in, trusted folders and saved approvals, so every session would start signed out.
--no-custom-instructions: it also turns off AGENTS.md, which is Plantoir's guidance.
--secret-env-vars: it does not stop Copilot's own sign-in reading GH_TOKEN, so it is no answer to the Windows environment note.
Accepting any executable called copilot (identity.why).
agents.serverEnvironmentWhy: Written as env beside args in mcp-{course}-copilot.json, as the Claude door writes it, so the server holds an assist lease on the course the door was opened from (shared-rules.json -> doorCourseHold.whichDoors.copilot). The argv stays the folder alone (serverArguments).

stoppedAtOnce.sentence: GitHub Copilot stopped as soon as it started. It may need updating: open it once on its own, or ask for help.
stoppedAtOnce.why: The door has already said it opened (the trail line is written when the window is handed over), so a Copilot that stops at once - an argument it does not know, a start-up failure - would otherwise leave a window holding Copilot's own 'unexpected argument' error, which names its help and tells a teacher nothing. The mac's script prints this sentence after Copilot exits with a status from 1 to 127 within withinSeconds of starting; measured, an unknown flag exits 1 in 0.07 s. A status of 128 or more is a signal, such as the teacher's own Control-C, and is not this failure (review L1: a stub killed by SIGINT at once printed the sentence before the fix). The window's own text, so rule 1 applies. Not measured: what Copilot's exit status is when the teacher answers No to folderTrust within the first seconds (the hand test). Claude's and Codex's doors have the same gap and are not changed here.

agents.timeoutWhy: Copilot's timeout on a local server, in milliseconds, covers tool discovery and every tool call (its schema: 'Timeout in milliseconds for tool discovery and tool calls'). With none, 1.0.108 falls back to 60 seconds (W0=6e4 in cli-main.js's callTool, read from the bundle 2026-11-13, not yet measured with a slow tool), and deploy_section is awaited and a first deploy takes minutes: Copilot would tell the model the deploy failed while Plantoir was still deploying. 1800000 is thirty minutes, as Codex's tool_timeout_sec=1800. Known limit: the same key covers tool DISCOVERY (Copilot's changelog: 'MCP server timeout settings now apply to tool discovery, with a 30-second default'), so a Plantoir server that hangs while starting would keep Copilot waiting up to thirty minutes for its tools; whether that holds up the prompt is not measured.
agents.writesNothingElse: Both files are in the app's own data directory. Nothing is written into the teacher's working folder, and nothing is added to or read from their own Copilot configuration.
agents.onWindows: Windows starts copilot.exe by argument vector, or npm's copilot.cmd through cmd /k as its other doors do, and passes the same arguments with the file's path; it must never ADD a GitHub token (COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN, GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN) to the child's environment, since Copilot signs in from any of them ahead of the teacher's stored sign-in. The mac never passes Plantoir's environment on: the script runs in the teacher's own Terminal or iTerm.

outsideAgents.courseIsNamedInTheGreetingOnly: The server is given the WORKING FOLDER, never a course, so every course in the folder is reachable from either door. What points a session at one course is the greeting. Both doors ALSO name their course to the server, in its environment (doorCourseVariable) - to HOLD it, never to narrow: the server takes an assist lease on it (shared-rules.json -> doorCourseHold), and every course stays reachable. This is a real difference from the assistant Plantoir carries itself, whose window is bound to one section and refuses any other course (assist-cases.json -> windowBinding), and it is stated here because a reader who assumed otherwise would give a door a narrowing it does not have.
outsideAgents.doorAssistantVariableWhy: #783 (Russell, 2026-11-13: the busy sentences name the assistant that is working on the course). Every door writes its own key (claude, codex, copilot: each agent's key) beside doorCourseVariable in its server's environment (each agent's serverEnvironment), and the server writes it as its assist lease's fifth line (file-formats.json -> workLease.lines), so another program's sentences can name it (shared-rules.json -> doorCourseHold.naming). Unset, or a key no door has, names none: the sentences then list all three, which is still true. Windows' doors and plantoir-mcp owe it (#783's windows issue); until then a Windows hold names none.
outsideAgents.doorCourseVariableWhy: The one name both platforms read: both doors write it into their server's environment (each agent's serverEnvironment: the Claude door in its configuration's env, the Codex door as a -c override), and the server - Plantoir --mcp-stdio on the mac since #458, plantoir-mcp on Windows since #430 - holds an assist lease on that course when the folder has it. An environment variable rather than an argument because the argv is the folder alone (serverArguments) and #430's trap was a course in the argv being read as a lock.

fixWith.fixGreetingIsOneLine: A command line cannot carry a newline (Windows starts an npm shim through cmd /k, and the mac's script is one line per command), so rows are numbered on one line (1) … · 2) …) rather than set one per line (plan review, MED 9), and with no semicolon anywhere (replaceInTheMessageWhy).

each handed row's prompt, verbatim, numbered
for a row with a page, the page's place from the working folder (courses/<COURSE>/<page>.md), and that the page is shared by every section when it is not under section<N>/

fixWith.closingWhy: A preview clears every problem but Cloudflare's refusal: a preview never runs that check and carries the row unchanged (shared-rules.json -> sectionProblems.deployRefusals.filesTooLargeForCloudflare.carryOver), so only a deploy clears it. closingPreview when every handed row is cleared by a preview, closingDeploy when every one is a deployOnlyKinds row, closingBoth otherwise (717b review M1).
fixWith.replaceInTheMessageWhy: A double quote would end the argument's quoting (greetingCarriesNoDoubleQuotes). A semicolon would split it wherever Windows Terminal reads the command line: it treats EVERY ; as the start of a new tab's command, inside quotes too (microsoft/terminal #13264; the documented escape is \;), so the message would open cut short and its tail as a second tab (717b review H1). Since Windows 1.9.3 (#736) neither Windows door puts Windows Terminal in front of the program, so the replacement is no longer load-bearing there; it is kept because the message is the same on both platforms. No piece of fixGreeting has a semicolon, and any a row brings - a TeX error, a sentence - is written as a comma. Each replacement keeps the length.
fixWith.skillForKindWhy: Each skill is one of the guidance skills the app writes into the working folder (support/agent_guidance/skills). Figures and GeoGebra sketches are plantoir-math-graphs, which knows what this site can draw; Swift and runnable code plantoir-runnable-code; self-check questions plantoir-quizzes; a handout plantoir-printing; everything else - links, page settings, a front page, the curriculum map, a file too large - plantoir-page-authoring, which the others defer to.
fixWith.charactersAre: Every count here is in characters as the mac's Swift counts them (String.count: grapheme clusters - one emoji, one accented letter, is one). Windows counts UTF-16 units (String.Length), which can be more for the same text (an emoji is two, and a family emoji is many), and cmd's 8,191-character limit is in UTF-16 units: so Windows applies the same bounds in Swift's characters where it can (StringInfo text elements), and must ALSO keep the whole command line's UTF-16 length under 8,191 - the 1,691 left over by 6,500 is the margin for that, measured with the longest greetingCases case (717b review L1). When Windows' own UTF-16 bound bites before the character bound, it drops rows from the END and says so with the `more` clause, exactly as the character bound does (717b fixes review L2).
fixWith.boundsWhy: The course name is cut at courseNameMaxCharacters (with …), so the bound holds whatever the course is called (717b review L2). Rows are named in the record's order until mostRowsInThePrompt are, or until the next would take the WHOLE message past greetingMaxCharacters; the first is always named, and the rest are 'and N more on the Problems tab'. A row's prompt is at most 400 characters (sectionProblems.prompt) and its page place at most pagePlaceMaxCharacters (cut with …), so ten ordinary rows fit, and 6,500 leaves room under cmd's 8,191-character command line for the terminal, the assistant's path and the configuration's.
rejected: Handing the rows over in a file the message names (plan review, MED 9's other option): it is a file written where the assistant can read it - the working folder, which Obsidian is watching - and nobody cleans it up; the one-line message fits.
One session per problem: a shared page's problems are one fix, and ten terminals are not triage.
Greying a button when its assistant is not installed: hiddenWhenNotInstalled, as Revise With ▸.
Asking a shell where the tool is: slow (1.06 s for zsh -lic on the planning Mac), and it runs the teacher's login scripts while a view draws. The doors' own search list (searchedForInOrder) is used.
