outsideAgents.handedToATerminal: The mac writes an executable .command script into the app's own data directory and hands it to iTerm (when it is already running) or Terminal, through LaunchServices rather than AppleScript so that no Automation permission is asked for. Windows has no such file. Since 1.9.3 (#736) both its doors start the program DIRECTLY when it is an .exe - by argument vector, with no command interpreter and no Windows Terminal in front, in a console window of its own (Windows Terminal anyway where it is the default terminal) - and through cmd.exe /v:off /s /k when it is an npm .cmd shim, with cmd's metacharacters escaped per parse and every % followed by a quote. Until 1.9.3 the Claude door ran wt.exe -d <folder> cmd /k with a hand-joined line, which left the greeting, and the course's name in it, outside cmd's quotes; and Windows Terminal itself was measured expanding %NAME% and re-joining arguments with its own quoting, which is why it is no longer in front of either door (documentation/12-windows-app.md -> 'What the outside doors hand to Windows, and how'). The SCRIPT is therefore the mac's mechanism, which is why it is listed separately from what is written for the CONNECTION.
outsideAgents.hiddenWhenNotInstalledWhy: A teacher who does not have the tool is not shown the menu item at all, rather than being shown one that is greyed out or that opens onto an error. Each door is hidden INDEPENDENTLY: a teacher sees an item for each assistant installed, in the order Claude, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and with none installed sees no sign that any exists.
outsideAgents.menuItemWhy: Each agent's menuItem is the item's title INSIDE Revise With ▸ — in the menu bar's Course and Section menus and, since the HIG sweep (#457 item 4, 2026-10-08), in every course and section row's context menu as well, so one command has one name everywhere (HIG: stable command names). Until the sweep the row's context menu showed it at the top level as 'Revise with Claude…' / 'Revise with Codex…' while the menu bar said Revise With ▸ Claude…, and this key held the context menu's words. 'Revise with Claude' is still the command's name in a SENTENCE (shared-rules.json -> workspaceWait's agent names, the support page); only the menu item's title moved. Windows draws its own menu, so it chooses where the item sits, but the item's words are these.
outsideAgents.neverInstalled: Plantoir never installs an outside assistant and never offers to. These are developer tools with accounts, sign-ins and their own update paths; an app that puts one onto a teacher's machine has taken on a support surface nobody wants, and the teacher has not agreed to it. The door opens onto something they chose to install themselves.
outsideAgents.neverProbedForSignIn: Finding the tool says nothing about whether the teacher is signed in to it, and the door does not try to find out: that would mean running the tool while a context menu is being drawn. A teacher who is signed out meets their assistant's own sign-in step inside the terminal, which is where it belongs.
outsideAgents.note: The OUTSIDE doors: handing one course to a command-line assistant the teacher already has on their own machine, so it can work on their pages through Plantoir's MCP server. Distinct from the assistant Plantoir carries itself (contracts/assist-cases.json), which runs on the teacher's machine with no account and no CLI. AUTHORED, not generated. announcedAddress.capturedAs: Each line is read as it ARRIVES, with an unfinished line carried over to the next piece of output and colour codes taken out one whole line at a time; the last announcement wins. Never read back off the end of the output, and never inferred from a port.
announcedAddress.measured: GitHub #235, on one real first preview (the mac, 2026-09-20 capture, ICS4U): the announcement is 6,055 characters in and about 11,000 more follow, so an 8,000-character tail had lost it by the time Quartz said its server started. Read a piece at a time with NOTHING carried over, cutting the line after ':8', ':81' or ':810' gives a valid address on the wrong port (3 of the line's cut points), and reading a raw piece of terminal output whole gives the right port with a garbage path ('http://127.0.0.1:8101/%0D%0A…') because the CRLF line ending is not split.
announcedAddress.whenTheLauncherCannotReadIt: preview.sh asks for this folder's published port twice; if both answers are empty it says it could not find out where the preview will be and stops before building (exit 1). It never announces the port inside the builder in its place. A build for publishing (--build-only) announces nothing and asks nothing, so it can never be stopped here.
announcedAddress.why: The port the builder uses inside is the same on every Mac, and the one this Mac opens is not: the first working folder publishes 8081 -> 8081, the next 8091 -> 8081, and so on. A guessed address is right by luck for the first folder only, and can open ANOTHER section's preview as though it were this one.

bindsTo.how: Every published address of a folder's workspace - the four site addresses and their four live-reload websockets - is published as `-p 127.0.0.1:<base>-<base+3>:8081-8084 -p 127.0.0.1:<base+1000>-<base+1003>:9081-9084`, from create_the_workspace_on_free_ports in the PREVIEW PORT BLOCK, so setup.sh, preview.sh and deploy.sh make it the same way and cannot remake it away from each other. A workspace made before #684 (every HostIp empty, which Docker reads as every interface) is remade once by setup.sh and preview.sh (every_published_address_is_this_macs_only, then whenTheWorkspaceIsInUse.sentences.whenItNeedsSettingUpAgain.forThisMacOnly and remake_the_workspace, so #94's wait and refusals apply). The check reads each binding in brackets, `[{{.HostIp}}]`: an old workspace's host address is EMPTY, and a check that every listed word is 127.0.0.1 passes it by finding no words. deploy.sh never makes this check: it never serves, and a publish at six in the morning should not pay a two-minute remake for it; it makes new workspaces the shared way, and a later preview remakes the old one.
bindsTo.measured: GitHub #684, 2026-10-31 and 2026-11-01, Colima 0.10.3 with its ssh forwarder, Docker 29.5.2, macOS 26. Before: every teaching-quartz-* workspace had HostIp "", and `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` showed `ssh ... *:8101` for each site and websocket address, so the preview answered from the Mac's address on the school network. With the prefix: lsof shows `127.0.0.1:<port>` only; `curl` to 127.0.0.1 and to localhost answers on the site and websocket addresses; `curl` to the Mac's network address and to [::1] is refused (exit 7) - and nothing listened on ::1 before either. `docker port` answers `127.0.0.1:<port>`, which preview.sh's announcement already reads (it keeps the text after the last colon). A block another workspace holds is still refused, in both directions (a loopback workspace onto an open one's block and the other way round), as `Bind for 127.0.0.1:<port> failed: port is already allocated`, which it_was_a_port_clash already reads. Nothing a teacher uses connects from anywhere else: the app's preview pane opens http://localhost:<port>/, Safari is handed 127.0.0.1, the reach check (#234) curls 127.0.0.1, and the live-reload client is ws://localhost:.
bindsTo.probe: hostBlockProbe is unchanged and still right: a port held by a program listening on 127.0.0.1 alone is in netstat's list as `127.0.0.1.<port>` and in lsof's as `127.0.0.1:<port>`, and both count it, so a localhost-only listener of somebody else's still makes a block taken. A same-account program on `*:<port>` can now sit beside this folder's `127.0.0.1:<port>` forward (127.0.0.1 still reaches the workspace, measured); the reach check's look for another account's listener counts sockets and remakes, which is conservative and correct.
rejected: Keeping the preview open on purpose, so it can be opened on an iPad or phone on the same Wi-Fi: nobody was found relying on it, and two of the preview-only packages (serve-handler, ws) carry denial-of-service advisories (#667's audit). If it is ever wanted it needs a setting a teacher turns on and a trail line, not a default.
Binding Colima's forwarder or Lima's hostIP instead: Colima is shared with other projects on this Mac (CLAUDE.md rule 7), and it would not cover Docker Desktop.

Serving Quartz on 127.0.0.1 INSIDE the workspace: Docker's forward connects to the workspace's own address, so the preview would stop answering at all (the reason Windows' loopback rewrite is native-only).

Remaking in deploy.sh too: it serves nothing, so an open address costs it nothing, and a scheduled publish keeps its warm builder. Measured (#684 review L2): a folder that only deploys keeps an old workspace's open forwards - lsof shows `ssh ... *:<port> (LISTEN)` - but with nothing serving, a request from the network gets an empty reply (curl exit 52) and no page; the next setup or preview makes it again on 127.0.0.1.
bindsTo.why: GitHub #684, found by #667's audit; Russell's decision 2026-10-31: localhost only. A preview is for the Mac that runs it; published on every interface, a running preview and its live-reload connection were open to anyone on the same network. Windows already binds its native preview to 127.0.0.1 (windows-app/Vendor/fetch-runtime.ps1, commit 2d32ca9e5, 2026-08-19, which rewrites both of Quartz's bind sites in handlers.js and, since #730, refuses to make a runtime unless both were rewritten), so this key is what both platforms do.

previewPorts.hostBlockCeilingWhy: Forty is a CHOSEN number, not a measured one. Any number up to 99 is possible - block 100's first port would be 9081, the first block's websocket - and forty keeps the walk under 8888 while the websockets (9081-9474) land only on the x1-x4 of each ten, clear of 9090, 9200 and 9229. A ceiling at all keeps the refusal REACHABLE, so it can be tested and its sentence stays true. Until GitHub #280 (2026-09-25) the launchers tried six blocks and stopped: six working folders' workspaces alive on one Mac - agent worktrees did it first, but a teacher who has used six working folders on a Mac does it too, since a workspace exists (and, before the second pass, kept its block) until something removes it, and nothing removes another folder's - and a seventh folder could neither preview nor publish. Every launcher walks the SAME forty for every run, publishing included: a workspace is made once per folder and serves both, and one made without ports for a publish would have to be remade by the next preview, killing anything running in it and discarding its warm copy of the website builder (109 s cold on a teacher's Mac, #225).

hostBlockClash.saysWhenAStartIsRefused: ❌ Plantoir could not start the website builder for this folder. Try again, or restart this Mac if it happens again.
saysWhenAStoppedWorkspaceIsRemade: ♻️  Something else is now using this folder's preview addresses, so Plantoir is setting this folder up again on free ones.
The next preview will be slower than usual — about two minutes — while it gets ready.
hostBlockClash.saysWhenCreationClashes: ↪️  Those preview addresses were taken a moment ago; trying the next ones…
hostBlockClash.saysWhy: The three things a launcher says in the console on these paths, written in each launcher's shared PREVIEW PORT BLOCK and checked against these keys by scripts/test_port_blocks.py. Mac-only: they are about a workspace, which the native (Windows) preview does not have. The remade line names its cost because the warm website builder lives inside the workspace and is lost (109 s cold, #225). The remade lines are said for all three causes of a remake on free addresses - a Docker refusal at start, a listener on a stopped workspace's port, and (#310) a RUNNING workspace whose announced address turned out to be somebody else's (whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress) - because to a teacher they are one event; the key keeps its name because two tests read it. saysWhenAStartIsRefused said "this folder's workspace" until 2026-09-29 (GitHub #381, #378's finding that the word meant nothing to Russell); it names the website builder now.
hostBlockClash.whenCreating: The probe and the creation are two steps, so two launchers starting together can both see a block free. When the creation is refused in any of these words the half-made workspace is removed WITHOUT force and the walk goes on from the NEXT block, up to the same ceiling. Any other refusal keeps the sentence it had.
hostBlockClash.whenStarting: A stopped workspace whose block has been taken since cannot start. Refused in any of these words - and ONLY these - it is removed without force and made again on free ports, and the console says the next preview will be slower (about two minutes: its warm copy of the website builder is gone). Any other refusal stops the run with the engine's own words and a sentence; before #280, setup.sh and deploy.sh stopped there with the engine's words alone and preview.sh carried on to fail later at a step that could not say why. Since #310 a stopped workspace is also LOOKED AT before it starts, by preview.sh only (WORKSPACE_WILL_SERVE) and under Colima only (whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress.gate): Colima does NOT refuse a start onto a port another account holds - it exits 0 and its forward silently fails (measured with root's 5900) - so a listener, in any account, on one of the workspace's own ports means the same remake, made before the start. A stopped workspace listens on nothing: its own forward is gone 0.011 s after the stop returns and back 0.011 s after a start (5 of 5 each way, development Mac), so the listener is somebody else's. Before removing anything it asks once more whether the workspace is RUNNING (another launcher for this folder started it a moment ago, and the listener is its own forward): then it is used as it is. setup.sh and deploy.sh never serve, so a squatted forward costs them nothing, and they keep their warm builder rather than pay the remake - a publish at six in the morning is not made slower or given a new way to fail. It is recorded as the before-start outcome of shared-rules.json -> activityTrail.mustRecord."preview address held by another account". The remake that follows a Docker REFUSAL writes nothing on the trail, as before.
hostBlockClash.why: Colima says 'port is already allocated'; Docker Desktop says 'Ports are not available: ... bind: address already in use'. The launchers use any working engine as-is, so matching only Colima's would give a Docker Desktop teacher the old broad sentence for a clash the walk could have stepped past.

hostBlockPasses.counts: every port listening on this computer, and every port published by another working folder's workspace, RUNNING OR STOPPED
every port listening on this computer, and every port published by another working folder's RUNNING workspace - so a block a stopped workspace was keeping can be taken
hostBlockPasses.when: only when the first pass found no block

previewPorts.hostBlockPassesWhy: The first pass keeps a stopped workspace's block for it, so the folder it belongs to starts again on its own addresses with its warm website builder. The second exists because nothing removes another folder's workspace: without it a block would be kept for ever by a folder that was moved, renamed or deleted (a workspace is named after its folder's path, so it can never be started again), and neither remedy whenNoBlockIsFree names - closing the other folders' windows, restarting the Mac - would free anything, since both only STOP workspaces. A stopped workspace whose block was taken this way is remade on free ports when its own folder next starts it (hostBlockClash.whenStarting). A native preview (Windows) has no workspaces, so both passes are the same for it; cases with stoppedBlocks describe workspaces and do not apply there.
previewPorts.hostBlockProbe: A block is taken if ANY of its eight ports (base..base+3 and base+1000..base+1003) is listening on this computer, IN ANY ACCOUNT, or is published by ANOTHER working folder's workspace - stopped ones included in the first of two passes (hostBlockPasses), since a stopped workspace listens on nothing yet needs its block back when it starts. On the mac the listening ports are read from TWO listings, each once for all forty blocks rather than one question per port (0.123 s per port for the old probe, 9.8 s for forty blocks): the kernel's own list, `netstat -an -p tcp`, which shows every owner's listeners (0.00-0.01 s measured), and this account's `lsof` listing (0.06-0.12 s). Until #310 it was `lsof` alone, which run as the teacher lists only the teacher's own programs: root's listeners (kdc on 88, screen sharing on 5900) and ANOTHER signed-in account's preview were invisible, so a second account on one Mac was handed 8081 while the first account's preview held it, its forward failed silently, and its Preview opened the other person's site (the #204 rehearsal). Only LISTEN rows count - a port in TIME_WAIT or ESTABLISHED is not a listener - and the port is the text after the LAST dot of netstat's local address (`*.8081`, `127.0.0.1.8443`, `::1.8443`; a long IPv6 address is cut short with its port kept, measured). Each listing that cannot be read counts as empty ON ITS OWN, so a netstat whose columns change in a future macOS falls back to exactly the old lsof answer, not to 'nothing listening'. The host listing is the only guard against another APP: Docker publishes over a port a program on the Mac already holds (measured: exit 0; under Colima even across accounts, with `docker port` naming the port anyway). Case fields: busyBlocks and busyPorts are listening in THIS account (both listings show them); anotherAccountBlocks and anotherAccountPorts are listening in another account or as root (only the kernel's list shows them); notListening rows are in the kernel's list in a state other than LISTEN; kernelListFails and accountListFails make that listing unreadable; stoppedBlocks are other folders' stopped workspaces. A NATIVE preview (Windows, and build_site.py's own re-probe there) binds ONE site port and its websocket rather than publishing a block of four, so it walks the same forty steps from the port it was asked for and checks only that pair (build_site.first_free_preview_port): of hostBlockCases, the ones made only of whole blocks - busyBlocks and anotherAccountBlocks, with or without a listing marked unreadable - apply to it as written, since a port is busy whoever holds it (whether Windows' own probe SEES another account's listener is the question the windows issue from #310 asks); the busyPorts and anotherAccountPorts ones describe a published block, the notListening ones describe the mac's kernel list, and the stoppedBlocks ones describe workspaces.
previewPorts.note: Several previews run at once, one per working folder, and they must not collide. These numbers are the toolchain's, not either app's: the container publishes fixed ports and the host side probes a block.

whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress.appliesOnWhy: PERMANENT, the same case as whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder: Windows' preview.ps1 serves on the PC itself, with no forward to lose, so there is nothing to find. Whether the Windows WALK sees another account's listeners is a different question, asked in the windows issue from #310.

cases.why: A healthy Colima Mac: one listener on the port, and it is this account's own forward.

The #204 rehearsal: the forward did not bind because another account holds the port, and the reach check was answered by THEIR forwarder. Remade once on free addresses; the new address is ours, and it is the one announced.
Still somebody else's after the remake (a race, or a listener that followed): stopped before building with the sentence, and never remade a second time.

Our IPv4 forward bound, but another listener sits beside it on ::1 - and localhost, the address the app opens, tries ::1 first and reaches THAT one (measured with a same-account stand-in). Counting rows rather than asking 'is one of them ours' is what catches it.
A refused connection is #234's case and is said as #234 says it; whose address it is is never asked.
This account's own list came back EMPTY: under Colima this account always owns limactl's listeners, so an empty list means lsof did not work, and nothing is proven. Goes ahead.
No lsof on this Mac: the question cannot be put, so nothing is refused over it.
The kernel's list cannot be read: nothing is proven, so it goes ahead as it did before #310.
Another engine: its forwarder was never measured, and Docker Desktop refuses a held port outright, so nothing is asked.
DOCKER_HOST names an engine that is not Colima (a developer's setting; the app never sets it): the check is off, and the trail says it was not made rather than going quiet.
DOCKER_HOST pointing into ~/.colima/ is still Colima, whatever `docker context show` says with it set, so the check is made.
A build for publishing opens no preview, so nothing is asked.

whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress.casesFields: looks: one entry per ownership look, in order - kernel is how many LISTEN rows the kernel's list (netstat) has on the announced port, or 'fails'; own is how many this account's list (lsof) has, 'empty' when that whole list is empty, or 'missing' when there is no lsof (this account always has another listener besides, limactl's, unless it is empty or missing). reach is curl's exit for the reach check (whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder). remakes is how many times the workspace was remade. portAfterRemake is the host port the remade workspace publishes. markers are the outcomes of the PLANTOIR_PREVIEW_ADDRESS_HELD lines printed, in order. netstatAsked says whether the kernel's list was read at all. outcome: announces (the address in announces), refuses (sentence, exit 1, nothing announced), reachRefuses (#234's refusal), asksNothing.
whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress.gate: Colima only, read ONE way for this check and for the look before a stopped workspace starts (hostBlockClash.whenStarting): DOCKER_HOST, when set, counts as Colima only if it points into ~/.colima/ or into $COLIMA_HOME (with DOCKER_HOST set, `docker context show` says 'default' whatever the engine); otherwise `docker context show` is colima or colima-<profile>. The app never sets DOCKER_HOST. A DOCKER_HOST naming anything else switches the check off and says so on the trail (the unchecked marker), so a check that silently stopped happening cannot pass for one that found nothing.
whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress.measured: Development Mac (Apple silicon, macOS 26 / Darwin 25.6, Colima 0.10.3 + Lima 2.2.0 - the versions setup.sh pins - vmType vz, portForwarder ssh), 2026-09-26, reproduced by the plan's review: `lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN` listed this account's 13 listeners; `netstat -an -p tcp` listed 17, including root's kdc on 88 and screen sharing on 5900. `docker run -p 5900:8081` while root held 5900: exit 0, `docker port` said 0.0.0.0:5900, Lima's ha.stderr.log said 'failed to set up forwarding tcp port 5900' at level warning with ssh exit 255, and curl to 127.0.0.1:5900 reached screen sharing (exit 1, not 7). `docker start` onto the held port: exit 0, the same silent failure. The forwarder for a published port is this account's own `ssh` (plus limactl on 53 and 127.0.0.1:49726, so a working lsof is never empty under Colima). A ::1-only listener beside our IPv4 forward: both bound; `curl http://localhost:P` reached the OTHER server, `curl http://127.0.0.1:P` ours. NOT measured: a listener owned by another ORDINARY account (no second account or sudo here). Root is a different uid, and XNU's check compares uids, so it stands in; the acceptance is Russell's two-account rehearsal.
whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress.probe: preview.sh only, after the reach check (whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder) passes and BEFORE the address is announced or anything is built, under the gate only: the address is somebody else's when the kernel's list has MORE listening sockets on the announced host port than this account's list has, and this account's list is not empty. Counts rather than presence, so a listener in another account on ::1 beside our IPv4 forward is caught too. Only the site port is looked at: a shadowed live-reload port costs only the page refreshing itself, and #234 declined the same widening for the same reason; the walk and the look before a start cover all eight. When it is somebody else's the workspace is remade ONCE (the remade marker is printed only after the remake RETURNS, so a remake #94 refused leaves #94's trail line and no claim of a rebuild), through the same remake every launcher uses (whenTheWorkspaceIsInUse: an open preview of another section from this folder refuses with its own sentence), the address is asked for again, reached again, and looked at again. Still somebody else's: the sentence, the refused marker, exit 1, nothing announced - the shape the app already treats as a preview that never appeared (#235), so the app needs no change. A build for publishing (--build-only) announces nothing and asks nothing.
rejected: A bind probe (the issue's first suggestion): it does see other accounts, even with SO_REUSEADDR, but it needs an interpreter - /usr/bin/python3 on a Mac without the Command Line Tools is a stub that opens the 'install developer tools' dialog - and one process per port cost 2.23 s for forty blocks. It also answers the wrong question both ways: without SO_REUSEADDR a port in TIME_WAIT (a preview closed a minute ago) reads as taken; with it, a same-account listener on another address reads as free (both measured).

A connect probe for the walk: 0.66 s for 320 ports, it sees only what answers on 127.0.0.1, and it knocks on other people's servers as a side effect. It stays where #234 put it: one connection, to our own announced port.
netstat alone, dropping lsof: a future change to netstat's columns would fail open to 'nothing listening', which is worse than before #310. The union costs 0.06 s.
Reading Lima's ha.stderr.log for 'failed to set up forwarding': the direct evidence, but an internal log in a Colima-version-specific place and JSON shape, and a Docker Desktop teacher has none.
Trusting `docker port`: measured to name 0.0.0.0:5900 for a forward that never bound (whenThePreviewNeverAppears.rejected says the same: it reports what it asked for).

Refusing at once, without a remake first: the teacher would hold a sentence whose remedies they may not be able to use (the other account is somebody else's session), while the fix is machinery that already exists and is tested.

Asking the system WHO owns the listener (netstat -v's process:pid, then ps -o user=): it would let the sentence tell another account from macOS, but the -v columns have moved between macOS releases, and it puts another person's username a step from this teacher's trail.

Looking before a stopped workspace starts in setup.sh and deploy.sh too: neither serves, so a squatted forward costs them nothing, and the look would give a six o'clock publish a two-minute remake and a new way to fail.
A per-port lsof (lsof -iTCP:<port>): 0.228 s a question (#234's number), and the counts need the whole list anyway.
sentence: Another account on this Mac — or macOS itself — is using the address this preview needs, so Plantoir stopped before building it.
Nothing is wrong with your pages. Press Preview to try again; if it happens again, restarting this Mac puts it right.
whenAnotherAccountHasTheAddress.why: GitHub #310, found in the #204 rehearsal: two macOS accounts on one Mac, each with Plantoir. The walk (hostBlockProbe) now sees another account's listeners, which prevents a NEW clash, but it cannot see another account's STOPPED workspace (its virtual machine is not ours to ask), so two accounts can still both hold 8081 on paper; whichever starts second is caught before its start (hostBlockClash.whenStarting), and this check catches the rest - a race, or a listing that failed - before a teacher is shown somebody else's site. The sentence names both things the check PROVES it could be (the kernel has a listener; this account owns none), rather than 'something'. 'Account' is a teacher's word, not machinery. Both remedies are true: a second press walks again past the listener; after a restart this account's workspace comes back STOPPED, and the look before a start catches the clash. Rejected wording: 'sign out of the other account' (the teacher may not be able to, and it names somebody else's session). Recorded on the trail as its own mac-only event, app-written from a marker (shared-rules.json -> activityTrail.mustRecord."preview address held by another account"). No machinery words (rule 1).

sentence: Every address Plantoir can use for a preview is taken.
Close Plantoir's windows for your other working folders, or restart this {machine}, then try again.
whenNoBlockIsFree.why: The old advice - 'stop another preview (or another app using ports 8081+)' - was false: a block belongs to a workspace that EXISTS, running a preview or not, and six idle workspaces held all six blocks on the development Mac. Closing a folder's last window stops its workspace, and a restart stops every workspace (they are made with no restart policy); the second pass of the walk (hostBlockPasses) then counts a stopped workspace's block as free, so both remedies the sentence names really do free room - a window closes for a folder open now, a restart for workspaces left running by a scheduled publish, the command line or a Plantoir from before 2026-09-19. What is left after both is ports other APPS are listening on. Printed by all three launchers - a PUBLISH that cannot get a workspace prints it too, which is why it says 'a preview' rather than naming what was pressed. Written on the trail as the launcher line of the existing 'preview did not appear' event (shared-rules.json -> activityTrail.mustRecord), not as a new event. No machinery words (rule 1).

cases.answer: the site answered inside the builder
cases.sentence:
Your website is built, and your website builder is serving it — but this Mac cannot reach it.

Nothing is wrong with your pages. Something on this Mac has stopped passing your website through. Restarting your Mac puts it right.
cases.why: The site answering inside while this Mac cannot reach the same site is PROOF rather than inference, and it is the only one of the three that can say what to do: restarting the Mac is the remedy that was watched working on the machine that met this.

cases.answer: the builder replied and nothing was serving the site inside it
cases.sentence:
Your website did not come up, so Plantoir stopped waiting for it.

Nothing has been lost. Press Preview to try again — and if it happens again, restarting your {machine} usually puts it right.
cases.why: The builder was reached and answered about a port with nothing on it, so the site really was not being served. Only a REPLY counts here - an answer that never arrived is the third case, not this one.

cases.answer: the question could not be put, or nothing came back from putting it
cases.sentence:
Plantoir could not get your website to appear, and could not tell why.

Nothing has been lost. Press Preview to try again — and if it happens again, choose “Report a Problem…” from the Help menu so somebody can see what happened.
cases.why: Added after review, because the first version asserted 'your website did not come up' for every answer that was not a site - the programs not being found, the builder gone, an engine that never replied inside the question's own deadline. A teacher can read `Started a Quartz server listening at …` in the console directly above that sentence, so it contradicts what is on their screen. An app that does not know says so, and points at the one thing that lets somebody else find out.

whenThePreviewNeverAppears.measured: On the development Mac, 2026-09-20: a site that answers inside the builder answers out here 0.026 s later, and one question put to the builder costs 0.03 s (five runs). On the Mac that met the fault, 2026-09-19: a first setup took 132.0 s and a first preview 109.3 s — which is why the RUN is never what is bounded.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.rejected: Bounding the whole run (a first preview legitimately takes minutes, so any bound short enough to help would refuse every teacher's first five minutes). Offering to restart the website builder from inside the app (another window, another copy of Plantoir or an outside assistant can be publishing in the same builder unseen, and the remedy was never measured to work). Believing what the builder says about which addresses it has published: it reports what it asked for, not what this Mac can reach, which is exactly how the fault stayed invisible.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.whatHappensToTheRun: It is STOPPED, the way the teacher's own Stop button stops it, and the port goes back through that path. Three things follow and all three are wanted: nothing is left serving a website nobody can see; the section stops reporting itself as building, which a wait that merely gave up would have said for ever; and the port is never handed to another preview while a live server still holds it.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.whatIsAskedAtTheEnd: The builder is asked whether the site answers INSIDE it, before anything is stopped — stopping ends the server the question is about. It answering while this Mac cannot reach the same site is the proof that the pages are fine and the Mac is not. There are THREE answers and not two, and the third is the one an implementation will forget: asked and answered (a site, or nothing), and not answered at all — the programs not found, the builder gone, an engine that never replied inside the question's own deadline. The third must never be reported as the second; see cases. On the mac that question is a request made inside the container; a platform whose preview does not run in one has no counterpart to build and should send only the first sentence's half it can prove.
whenThePreviewNeverAppears.whatIsBounded: The QUIET, not the run: no new output AND no answer, counted from the moment the builder says its server has started, and restarted every time more output arrives. A preview that is still printing is not stalled however long it has been going.

whenNoAddressWasAnnounced.why: GitHub #235. The launcher announces the address BEFORE it starts the build, and output is read in order, so once the builder has said its server started a missing address is final rather than late — the wait stops at once, the way the silence ending stops it (the run is stopped as the Stop button stops it, the alert shows the third sentence, the trail gets its own line). The builder is NOT asked: its question is about an address and there is none. Rejected: trying the section's own port (the port inside the builder, wrong for every working folder after the first — this development Mac's folder publishes 8091 for 8081); waiting on until the silence bound or the ten-minute bound (nothing is on its way, and a wait that gives up with the run still going leaves the section saying it is building for ever); a new sentence (the third one is exactly true).

whenThePreviewNeverAppears.why: GitHub issue #225. A teacher pressed Preview, the progress bar filled, the builder said its server was listening, and the app then waited ten minutes and said nothing at all — no sentence, no line on the trail, the section still reporting itself as building. The website was built and was being served the whole time; that Mac had stopped passing new addresses through. Every part of this rule exists because of one half of that: the bound is on the quiet because the run was not slow, the question is put to the builder because guessing between the two causes would have told a teacher their pages were broken when they were not, and the run is stopped because leaving it holding a port while saying nothing is the state the report was made about.

whenTheWorkspaceIsInUse.appliesOnWhy: PERMANENT: Windows builds natively — there is no `docker` in setup.ps1, preview.ps1 or deploy.ps1 — so it has no workspace to remake and nothing to wait for.

idRace.rule: Stopped and removed by the id read at the start. A remove that fails because that id is gone is no failure (another launcher removed it); a remove that fails with it still there is tried once more two seconds later, then the run stops with hostBlockClash.saysWhenAStartIsRefused. At the making, a refusal because a workspace by this name already exists (Docker: 'is already in use by container') waits two seconds, uses that workspace if it is running, else tries the making once more — and a second such refusal stops the run with the same sentence, never with the home-folder advice a mount refusal gets.
idRace.why: Two launchers remaking together (two previews started after an update) both find the old workspace idle. By NAME, the slower one's stop and remove landed on the NEW workspace the faster one had just made — #94's shape one step down. By id they land on the old one, already gone. Plan review 2026-09-25 (F4): without the conflict branch the slower launcher's `docker run` was refused with the name taken and told the teacher to keep their folder inside their home folder.

whenTheWorkspaceIsInUse.rule: Before ANY launcher removes this folder's workspace to make it again — for any of the reasons it has (made for another folder, no builds mount, an older recipe, no live-reload addresses, a courses folder it cannot write, a connection gone stale) — it looks at what is running inside it, and asks this Mac, for each piece of work, whether the program that OWNS it is still running (whatCountsAsRunning, GitHub #378). Nothing, or only work whose owner has gone: it is remade at once, and work whose owner has gone is ended with it and said (sentences.whenLeftoverWorkIsStopped, the trail's 'left-over work stopped'). A build, a publish or a course being set up whose owner IS running: it is waited for, looking every lookEverySeconds, naming what it waits for on the console and in the app's status line (PLANTOIR_WAITING_FOR), and refused after workSeconds, naming it again. A preview whose launcher is still running on this Mac: refused after previewSeconds, naming the preview. It is then stopped and removed BY ID, never by name and never with -f, and that stop is the ONLY way anything inside is ended. One function does all of this for every launcher, remake_the_workspace in the PREVIEW PORT BLOCK, and each of the launchers' twenty places that remade a workspace calls it; the old shared workspace (teaching-quartz) is retired only when nothing at all is running in it — leftovers included, since it is not this folder's — and otherwise left, silently.

leftovers.joined: Two are joined with " and "; three or more with ", " and a final " and ", in the order the marker lists them.
leftovers.setup: the setting up of a course

statusLine.preview: Waiting for the preview of {course} section {section} to close…
statusLine.somethingElse: Waiting for something else in this folder to finish…
statusLine.why: GitHub #378, decision 3: what a preview is waiting for is named in the STATUS LINE under the progress bar — no alert, nothing to dismiss, no need to open the details. Rendered by the app from PLANTOIR_WAITING_FOR (the launcher prints it beside its console sentence) with the same origins and doing words, and followed by the counter, which counts from the moment the wait began. PLANTOIR_WAITING_FOR: over, the next milestone reached, or the run ending gives the line back. 'Deploying', not 'publishing': it is the word on the button a teacher pressed.

whenAPreviewIsOpen: ❌ The preview of {course} section {section} from this folder is still open, and Plantoir needs to set this folder up again before it can go on.
Close that preview — in Plantoir, or wherever it was started — then try again. Nothing was changed.

whenItNeedsSettingUpAgain.forBuiltWebsitesOutside: ♻️  Setting this folder up again so built websites can be kept outside your course folder…

whatCountsAsRunning.casesWhy: `launchers` rows are either a command line (given pid 7001, 7002… and parent 1) or [pid, parent, command line], so a case can say who started what. `leftovers` is the space-separated WORKSPACE_LEFTOVERS the look must set, `waitingFor` its WORKSPACE_WAITING_FOR; both default to empty. `psFails` makes the process table unreadable. Run through the REAL look by scripts/test_port_blocks.py in all three launchers. `psEmpty` makes `ps` answer 0 with no lines. A course with a space is carried with "+" for it (`preview`, `waitingFor`, `leftovers` and the markers), and decoded for every sentence.
whatCountsAsRunning.knownLimits: The owner test is folder-blind: another working folder's launcher for the SAME course and section makes this folder's leftover count as owned (a needless wait, and the status line names that other folder's work, for up to ten minutes — the safe direction; matching by working directory was rejected as a second system query for a failure that only waits). Between the last look and the stop — tens of milliseconds — another launcher can start something in the workspace, which is then ended, and not named: narrowed, not closed. And a workspace remade during a deploy's host-side stretch (the token handed in, before the upload starts) has nothing inside to see. Closing those needs a lock every launcher and the app honour, which is what #156's work leases are for, and they are the app's. A course code shaped like "ABC --1" (a space then two dashes) would be cut at the dashes when the look reads --course; CourseCodeRule allows one space but a code beginning a word with "--" is not a code anyone writes, and the cost would be a preview read as left over — recorded rather than guarded (#378 fix-round review N2). A course code outside CourseCodeRule — which no app and, since #402, no command-line setup can make, but which a course made at the command line before #402, or a folder given a course_config.json by hand, can still carry — is misread here in the DAMAGING direction (#388 impl review S3, measured with a pretend ps on the branch and on dev alike): a letter outside A-Z ("CAFÉ") is not matched by the scheduled-deploy label rule, so a publish set for later of that course, in the moment only its runner is left, reads as gone and can be ended; and a "+" ("C++") is read back as a space, so even a live deploy.sh of that course reads as gone. Work holding ";" or "\" is answered every piece owned instead (a case for each). Narrowed by #402, not closed: the command-line setup applies CourseCodeRule since then (course-management.json → courseCode.commandLine), and a course that already carries such a code is renamed in the app.
whatCountsAsRunning.originsWhy: Who started the owner, read from its ancestors: 'scheduled' first (the app's --run-scheduled-deploy runner is the Plantoir binary with no --mcp-stdio, so it must not be read as a window — plan review N2), then 'claude' / 'codex' / 'assistant' for a Plantoir --mcp-stdio with claude, codex or neither above it, then 'window' for the Plantoir app, then 'claude' / 'codex' for one of them running the launcher directly, and otherwise 'terminal'. '-' when the table could not be read.
whatCountsAsRunning.rule: One look answers one of three: 'nothing' (not running, gone, only its own first process, or only work whose OWNER has gone), 'a preview' (build_site.py WITHOUT --build-only, with everything it started, AND a preview.sh for that course and section running on this Mac other than this run), or 'other work' (a build, a publish, a course being set up or anything else whose owner is running, and a running workspace that `docker top` did not answer). Every process belongs to the OUTERMOST piece of work above it inside the workspace: deploy.py (the `sh -lc` wrapper and the Python both name it) is a publish of its --course and --section, and the build_site.py --build-only a deploy runs as its own child is part of that publish (#378 plan review S2). The owners, proved from the LIVE process table only: a preview — preview.sh C S without --stop or --build-only; a build — preview.sh C S --build-only, or deploy.sh C S; a publish — deploy.sh C S; a course being set up — setup.sh; anything else — any launcher. Belts, for everything but a preview: a publish set for later, by the scheduled script's name, ca.russellgordon.Plantoir.deploy.<CODE>.section<N>[.<folder id>].sh, ending .sh (the course written as ScheduledDeploy.sanitizedCode writes it — previewWhileItsSectionDeploys.labelCodeCases) and, for anything else, any such script; and a live `docker exec` aimed at this workspace by name or id. An open preview wins over other work, because waiting cannot end it. A website builder serving with no build_site.py above it is always left over. The table is read by ONE reader, the_launchers_running in the PROCESS TABLE BLOCK every launcher carries, which preview.sh's guard (previewWhileItsSectionDeploys) asks too (#388): the two share how a launcher, its course and section, its flags and a publish set for later are recognised, and when the table is unreadable; each keeps its own policy. This look counts a launcher a line merely NAMES (the guard counts only the program), and any flag on it for a publish or a build, on purpose: `bash -x ./deploy.sh C S` is a running publish whose program word is a flag away — counting too many costs a wait, counting too few ends a publish.
whatCountsAsRunning.whyTheLauncherIsAsked: Measured 2026-09-25 (plan review) and again 2026-09-29 for #378: killing the host side of `docker exec` leaves the process running inside the workspace, parented to the engine's shim — and under `docker exec -it`, which is how every launcher the app starts runs (on a pseudo-terminal), an in-container process waiting for an answer waits for ever (`read` from a terminal, still there minutes later), while one that is still working finishes on its own. That is how work is left behind when the app is force-quit, a Terminal window is closed or an assistant session ends. Counted as running, it refused every remake of that folder after ten minutes, until the Mac was restarted — which is what #378 reported. So an owner is proved per piece of work, from the process table read once per look, by a live process whose own command line names the same launcher, course and section: never by a remembered process number (no lease file, no pid file, no `kill -0`), so a number reused by another program cannot keep a dead owner alive. The course is matched in either case, the section exactly; this run, its ancestors and its descendants are left out (a login shell wrapping it carries the same words). An assistant session that is merely open owns nothing (#378 decision 1): it owns work only through a launcher it is running. A process table that cannot be read counts as every owner running: a wait and a refusal are recoverable, a publish ended is not. So does ANY other failure of the reader (#388): a caller that waited only on its "unreadable" answer would read a reader missing from the launcher — "command not found" — as every owner gone.

whenTheWorkspaceIsInUse.why: GitHub #94. Removing a workspace ends everything running inside it, and until this every one of those places stopped it without looking (setup.sh 8, preview.sh 5, deploy.sh 7, plus the three that retired the old shared workspace with -f). A preview open in one window died when another launcher in the same folder remade the workspace — after an update changed the recipe, once per folder for the builds mount, on a publish whose connection had gone stale — and a build or a publish half-way through was killed. The look is the app's own quit rule (documentation/09-mac-app.md: a workspace listing more than its first process is busy, and one that cannot be asked counts as busy), so the app and the launchers agree on what 'running' means. Measured on the development Mac 2026-09-25: an idle workspace lists exactly one process (tail -f /dev/null), `docker top` prints whole command lines, one look costs 23 ms, and a STOPPED workspace cannot be asked at all (exit 1) — hence 'stopped' is checked first. By id: two launchers started together can both find the old workspace idle, and a stop by NAME from the slower one would land on the new workspace the faster one has just made.

whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder.measured: Development Mac (Apple silicon, Colima vz aarch64), 2026-09-25: a connection to a forwarded port with nothing serving inside answers curl exit 52 in 0.01-0.03 s; to a port nothing listens on, exit 7 in 0.01 s; lsof -iTCP:<port> -sTCP:LISTEN takes 0.228 s. All 48 host ports published by six running workspaces had a listener. #225's own numbers: the listener appears 0.10-0.24 s after the builder is created or started, 0.15 s under load. NOT measured: the first address after the builder's virtual machine starts cold - hence the longer bound when this run started it, and the console line that reports the tries a slow reach took.
whenThisMacCannotReachTheBuilder.probe: preview.sh only, after the address is known and BEFORE it is announced or anything is built: a connection to 127.0.0.1 at the announced HOST port (never the port inside the builder), made with curl's own settings file ignored (-q, first) and no proxy (--noproxy '*'), at most one second each (--max-time 1). Only 'connection refused' (curl exit 7) counts as the builder being out of reach; every other answer - 0, an empty reply (52, what a healthy Mac gives, since nothing is served yet), a timeout (28), no curl at all (127), anything - goes ahead exactly as before. A build for publishing (--build-only) announces nothing and asks nothing. A run that needed more than one try prints reachedAfterRetrying in the console (not on the trail).

rejected: lsof as the probe: ten times slower, and run as the teacher it sees only the teacher's own programs - a listener owned by root (:88, kdc) is invisible to lsof and answers curl, so a forwarder owned by anybody else would read as missing and refuse a healthy Mac.
A check in setup.sh, at the builder's creation: it would not have fired on the night (all three previews met a builder that was already running), and setup is exactly the cold start nobody has timed.
A single probe: the cold start is unmeasured, so one refusal is not proof.
Asking inside the builder first: before the build nothing is served inside, so it proves nothing; that question stays whenThePreviewNeverAppears', after the build.
Checking the live-reload port as well: a Mac that refuses new forwards refuses both, and stopping a preview over live-reload alone would be a heavier answer than the fault.

Skipping the check when this run started the builder: the fault is an old virtual machine refusing new forwards, but one broken from birth would then build for minutes first; the longer bound catches both.

whenShown.when: a SYMLINKED page, or a page inside a symlinked folder, has changed
whenShown.why: FOUND BY REVIEW, and it had shipped wrong. A directory enumerator neither follows a symlink nor reports it as a regular file, so a `Media` folder symlinked into the teacher's Obsidian vault - the arrangement build_site.py's own _ensure_media_symlink exists for - contributed NOTHING and every change inside it read as up to date. whenShown.when: a page was restored from a backup that preserved its modification date and its size did not change
whenShown.why: A KNOWN, ACCEPTED false negative, written down so it is not discovered as a surprise. The fingerprint is of file metadata, never of file contents, which is what makes it cheap enough to run whenever a window comes to the front. `cp -p`, `rsync -a`, unzipping a backup and Time Machine all preserve modification dates, so restoring yesterday's version of a page can leave the marker off. The cure - hashing every byte of every page - costs more than the marker is worth. Publishing is never blocked by the marker, so the teacher can always publish anyway.

publishingDestinations.whyTheyDiffer: The new-course default and the meaning of a MISSING deploy_target are different on purpose. Every course written before the other destinations existed has no deploy_target and deploys to Netlify today; reading an absent key as Cloudflare would move a working class site to a host the teacher has no account with, at its next deploy, with nothing to say so. So the fallback stays Netlify everywhere it is read (CourseConfiguration.deployTarget, deploy.py --target, deploy.sh and deploy.ps1, build_site's domain resolution), and both apps' new-course windows WRITE deploy_target for every course they make, so the fallback only ever applies to a file that predates them. setup_course.py writes newCourseDefault for a course it makes with no saved file (since Russell's ruling of 2026-11-01), keeps a saved deploy_target when it is run again, and writes NONE over a saved file that names none — that course predates the other destinations and keeps deploying to Netlify. And a deploy typed at the command line goes where the course's settings say (Russell, 2026-11-01): deploy.sh, given neither --target nor --to-folder, reads deploy_target — absent still meaning Netlify — and deploys each additional destination as a leg of its own; a typed --target still wins. savedDestinations.note: GitHub #739 items 7 and 8 (Windows) and #668 (mac). A deploy given neither --target nor --to-folder reads the course's course_config.json and deploys where it says, as the app's Deploy button does: deploy_target absent, empty, null or "netlify" is --target netlify, "cloudflare_pages" is --target cloudflare, "local_folder" is --to-folder deploy_folder_path, and each additional_deploy_targets entry (an object with a non-empty text type) is a leg of its own after the main one. One destination: the launcher sets it and prints sentences.oneDestination. More than one: it runs ITSELF once per leg with every flag as typed plus that leg's flags, prints sentences.eachLeg before each, keeps going after a leg that fails or is refused (sentences.legRefused), and exits with the first failing leg's code. --reset-token looks only at the first. A settings file that is there and cannot be read refuses with sentences.couldNotRead and never falls back to Netlify; an absent one is left to the course-folder check. A typed --target or --to-folder wins and the file is not read. Because a flagless call now deploys every leg, the app names every leg it runs, Netlify included (deployArguments). Proposed from Windows on 2026-11-11: deploy.ps1's Get-SavedDestinations runs every case (windows-app/test_launcher_rules.ps1), and since #771 scripts/test_deploy_sh_destination.py runs every case against deploy.sh, through both of its readers (plutil and a Python). A tab, a carriage return or a line break in a kind or a path, at its end included, becomes a space, so each leg is one line (#771). {course}, {section}, {where} and {kind} are filled; {where} comes from sentences.where, and a kind not listed there reads as Netlify's word.

savedTokenCheck.note: GitHub #705 (Windows) and #716 (mac). A SAVED publishing token is checked before a deploy, and the check's answer is one of three words: accepted, refused, unheard. Only refused may clear the token (and, for Cloudflare, the remembered account); unheard keeps it, prints the two lines failureExplanations cases 13 and 14 lift, and stops the deploy with exit 1. refused means HTTP 400, 401 or 403 AND a body matching the service's refusedWhenTheBodyMatches; accepted means a 2xx AND a body matching acceptedWhenTheBodyMatches; everything else is unheard, status 0 (nothing answered) included. The PASTE checks are deliberately not this rule: a refused paste is not saved. Proposed from Windows on 2026-11-11 so the two launchers stop holding the rule in two tables; deploy.ps1's Get-TokenCheckAnswer runs every case (windows-app/test_launcher_rules.ps1), and since #771 scripts/test_deploy_token_refusal.py runs every case through deploy.sh's token_check_answer, and checks deploy.sh's addresses and patterns are these. documentation/07-deployment.md -> "A token Cloudflare refuses (#695), and a saved one is cleared only on a refusal (#716)".
savedTokenCheck.patternDialect: Each pattern is read by grep -E on the mac and by .NET's Regex on Windows, so it uses only what the two read IDENTICALLY: literal characters, bracket expressions of literal characters and ASCII ranges, and *. No \s, no \d, no escape inside a bracket (POSIX takes a backslash there literally), and no POSIX class: .NET reads [[:space:]] as a set of the characters [ : s p a c e, matching wrongly with no error. The spacing allowance is a bracket holding a real space and a real TAB character (the JSON \t). Matched case-sensitively.
